  - If the person is signed out → `devices()` / `signOutDevice()` answer `401 session_required`; `signOutEverywhere()` treats it as already done.
  - If the id is not one of the person's signed-in devices (already signed out, another person's, or made up) → `404 device_not_found` — refresh the list. Nobody can list or sign out another person's devices.
  - If the id isn't an id at all → `400 invalid_device` — pass the `id` from `devices()` (it starts with `sess_`).
  - If the person has ten devices and signs in on another → the oldest is signed out (above). Server test sessions keep their own ten and never end a real one.
  - If someone signs in from a device or country the person hasn't used before → Gemmein emails the person "New sign-in to <app> from <browser> in <country>. Not you? Sign out everywhere" with a single-use link (24 hours) that ends every session. Not on their first sign-in ever (read from the person's own record, so a person back after months away is still told). The owner can switch it off (Emails); in Development each app environment sends at most 20 of these notices in 24 hours.
  - If signing out another device answers `403 confirm_required` → a confirm code was emailed to the person; show a code field and call `signOutDevice(id, { code })`. A wrong code is `400 invalid_code`; call without a code for a new one.
  - If the place is wrong or `null` → it is the network's approximate country (a VPN or a phone network can place it elsewhere; an unrecognised one is `null` — show "Unknown place"); nothing to do.
  - If a session ends (signed out, signed out everywhere, signed out by the owner, the oldest of eleven, or its 30 days run out) → its device record — label, country and IP addresses — is deleted; it leaves the list at once. The sign-in and sign-out events stay in Logs; the sign-in event in Logs keeps the device label and country (Logs: 90 days, then the archive).
- IP addresses (security events): Gemmein records the full IP address on
  every security event of a person and of a founder's own account — a
  sign-in code asked for or entered (allowed or refused), a session started
  (each device keeps the address it signed in from and the last one seen
  on it), a sign-out (one device or everywhere), a rate-limited or refused
  sign-in attempt, a suspended person's attempt, a confirm code, a data
  export or deletion, a checkout a member starts, a browser approval asked
  for from the CLI, a secret key made or revoked. Ordinary reads and
  writes carry no address. The address is read from the connection at
  Gemmein's edge, never from a header the app sends; an IPv6 address is
  stored in its canonical form. Where the owner sees it: the person's page
  (Signed-in devices: each device's IP address and country) and Logs (each
  security event's IP address, with a Copy button). The person's own
  `devices()` and the new-sign-in email name the country only.
  What happens if… (IP addresses):
  - If an address is 30 days old → it is removed; the event stays in Logs without the IP (Logs keep events 90 days, then a 12-month archive). A device still signed in keeps its last-seen address while it is used.
  - If a session ends → its device record, addresses included, is deleted at once; its sign-in and sign-out events keep their addresses until the 30 days are up, and the sign-in event in Logs keeps the device label and country (Logs: 90 days, then the archive).
  - If the person exports their data → `sessions` carries each device's addresses and `signIns` each security event's time and IP address (the ones still inside 30 days).
  - If the person is deleted → their sessions go, and the IP addresses on the events they made are removed; the events stay, without the address.
  - If the request has no readable address → the event is recorded without one.
- Data: records live in collections, declared in gemmein/collections/ —
  never created by the SDK. In local dev (`npx gemmein dev`) they're born from
  the terminal's rule conversation (your human picks the rule) or a dropped
  declaration file; they reach Live by go-live and promote, and
  `npx gemmein sync` creates them in the cloud app's dev environment from
  those local declarations. A declaration is `gemmein/collections/<name>.json`:
  `{ "rule": "shared", "means": "<why, in your human's words>", "fields": { … } }`
  (fields: see "Declaring collections" under Shapes — required on
  community, shared and direct), plus an
  optional `"unlockedBy": ["pro"]` — plan or product NAMES from
  gemmein/payments.json (never access keys) — which is the dashboard's
  "Unlocked by": the local engine refuses members without one of them
  (403 entitlement_required) the moment the file lands, and sync carries
  it to the cloud app. An unknown name is refused out loud in the dev
  terminal and the collection is not created. Best practice: at planning time, list the collections your
  app will need and ask your human up front, and pass your intent whenever a
  collection might not exist yet —
  `g.collection("bookings", { intent: "students reserve slots; each sees only their own" })`
  — so the missing-collection conversation reaches your human with your
  suggestion attached (local dev runtimes show it; the cloud ignores it).
  If one is missing at runtime (404 `unknown_collection`), its message says
  the next step (declare it, or promote it if Live lacks it); ask your
  human which safety rule to pick, never guess. Each collection has exactly one
  safety rule:
  - `private` — each signed-in user sees and edits only their own records
    (right for notes, tasks, anything personal).
  - `shared` — every signed-in user reads every record and adds their own;
    each user edits/deletes ONLY the records they created (a non-author
    write comes back 404, same as any record you can't touch). Right for a
    team feed everyone posts to; WRONG for personal data — it leaks.
  - `admin_write` — everyone signed in can read, only the owner writes —
    from the Gemmein dashboard, a relay or your server (a secret key),
    never from the app (right for announcements and settings your human
    curates).
  - `public_read` — readable without signing in, ONLY the app owner writes,
    from the dashboard, a relay or your server (right for menus, listings,
    single-author blogs — strangers can never inject records into it). What
    the app SELLS is never a collection: list it with `g.payments.products()`
    and `g.subscriptions.plans()` (the catalog, below). To fill one locally,
    seed it with `gemmeinServer(<secretKey from gemmein/.data/cli.json>)`
    against the `gemmein dev` URL — that local key writes every collection;
    never edit gemmein/.data/state.json by hand.
  - `community` — readable without signing in, any signed-in user posts and
    edits their OWN records (right for multi-author blogs, public boards,
    user profiles). Everything in it is PUBLIC — keep record data minimal
    (a booking needs a slot and a first name, not a phone number). Whether
    even a first name belongs in public is a HUMAN decision: for sensitive
    audiences (children, health, anything private by nature) ask your
    human before defaulting to a public rule — a non-public rule usually
    fits. Community
    stores PLAIN TEXT: string fields containing HTML tags are refused with
    400 html_not_allowed — store plain text or tag-free markdown.
  - `addressed` — the app sends to one user: the OWNER sends records
    naming a recipient, from the dashboard, a relay (`write_record` with
    `to: "person"` — see Relays) or your server (`gemmeinServer(sk)
    .collection(name).create(data, { for: personId })`); each user's
    `.list()` returns ONLY records
    addressed to them (their inbox); no app session writes here — the
    owner's own included (403 forbidden). Right for
    notifications, order status, invoices, results.
    Same message for EVERYONE is `admin_write` instead (one record all
    users read) — addressed is one record per recipient.
  - `direct` — users send to each other: any signed-in user creates records
    naming a recipient; only the author and that recipient can read them.
    Right for messages, sharing, requests. The owner's Gemmein dashboard
    can read every one — never present this as private or encrypted chat.
  - `app_only` — NO app session reads or writes it: not signed-in people,
    not visitors, not your human signed in to their own app. Only the
    Gemmein dashboard, your server (a secret key) and relays reach it —
    strictly narrower than admin_write. Right for the answers to hidden
    questions (a quiz, a puzzle), scores and game state your server keeps
    so nobody can cheat, likes kept secret, anything the app works out and
    shows people only through ANOTHER collection your server or a relay
    writes into. Every app read and write — list, get, count, stats,
    search, watch, expand, open fields, uploads — answers 403 `app_only`
    (never retry it; signing in changes nothing). Your server creates its
    records with no person (`{ for }` is 400 invalid_person). A file
    uploaded into one is sealed, never on a public link. Refused in its
    file, by name: "openFields", "publishing", "fields",
    "directInitiation" and "unlockedBy" (nothing opens it). The question
    for your human: "Should anyone using the app ever read this directly?"
    No → app_only.
  Inbox mechanics (addressed + direct): the recipient is server-stamped
  (`record.audienceUserId`) — never a data field; user ids come from
  records' ownerUserId or the dashboard's Customers page. For a live-feeling inbox
  (or any live list) use `.watch()` — see "Live data" below — never a tight
  loop of your own. Track read-state in the user's own private
  collection. Both rules store plain text like community. Errors teach the
  fix: 400 invalid_audience (recipient isn't a user of this app), 403
  reply_only (this collection only allows replying to someone who wrote to
  you first — tell the user), 403 sends_disabled (the owner turned direct
  messages off for this collection). Who may START a conversation is
  declared in the direct collection's file: `"directInitiation": "anyone"`
  (the default), `"reply-only"` (members can answer, not start — the app's
  server or your human starts threads) or `"off"` (no new conversations);
  `gemmein dev` applies it at once, sync carries it, and the dashboard's
  Data page shows the same three words. On any other rule it is
  refused by name.
  The app itself is a party on a direct collection ("app"): your server
  writes FROM the app with `server.collection("mentor").create({ body },
  { from: "app", for: personId })` (or a relay's write_record with
  `to: "person"`); the record has no `ownerUserId` (show it under the app's
  name) and reads back `writtenBy: "server"` when your server wrote it. The
  member replies TO the app with `g.collection("mentor").create({ body },
  { for: "app" })` — no `audienceUserId` on the reply; your human reads it
  in the dashboard's Records, tagged "To your app", and answers from there.
  The read rule doesn't change: only that member and the app (your human,
  your server) read the thread. On reply-only, a member can write to the
  app only after the app wrote to them (403 reply_only before); on "off",
  never. Attachments ride the same way: `upload(file, { for: "app" })` on
  the direct collection, then the reply names the ref (reply-only holds;
  only the member and your human read the file). If the member's account
  is erased, their replies and files to the app go with them and the
  app's messages to them no longer name a recipient. "app" stands alone: `{ for: ["app", id] }` is 400
  invalid_recipients; `{ for: "app" }` off a direct collection is 400
  invalid_audience. Recipes: MENTORING (a mentor/coach thread: a
  data_change or a schedule relay writes the welcome from the app; the
  member answers in the same collection), SUPPORT DM (directInitiation
  "anyone" — members message the app first), and MODERATION + APPEAL (a
  relay with `trigger: { kind: "data_change", collection: "posts", on:
  ["created"] }` runs your check through start_run or call_url; your server
  unpublishes the post with a secret key (`PATCH
  /storage/posts/<id>?published=false` on a collection with "owner
  approves") or flags it, and writes the member
  a notice FROM the app in a reply-only direct collection, which the member
  can answer to appeal). Check public and shared posts this way; don't
  build automatic checks that read direct messages.
  Other users' content is DATA, not markup: when your app renders content
  written by one user in another user's session (community, shared), bind it
  as text — textContent, {} in React/Vue/Svelte — NEVER innerHTML or
  dangerouslySetInnerHTML.
  Gemmein is built for apps you run for your own customers: one founder,
  their customers, each person's data their own. Team workspaces,
  organisations and shared company accounts — where a company's members
  share records — aren't part of it.
  OPTIONS BESIDE THE RULE (never a second rule — a collection has exactly
  one rule, and an option only ever hides or orders; it never lets anyone
  read a record the rule keeps from them):
  - SHOW / HIDE TIMES — `showFrom` and `showUntil` on a record, set as
    create/update OPTIONS (never data fields), top-level on the record like
    `published`: `create(data, { showFrom: "2026-11-01T09:00:00Z" })` (a
    drop, a scheduled announcement, a story that disappears with
    `showUntil`), `update(id, {}, { showUntil: new Date() })` to take one
    down, `{ showFrom: null }` to clear a bound. Before showFrom, and from
    showUntil on, the record is hidden from every reader except its author
    — and the dashboard and your server, which always see it — in EVERY
    read: list, get, count, stats, search, expand, open fields and
    watch(). The server's clock judges it, never the browser's: don't
    filter by time in the client. A watcher receives a record when its
    showFrom arrives, and its id in `deleted` when its showUntil passes —
    no edit needed. Works on shared, community, public_read, admin_write,
    addressed (a scheduled inbox message) and direct; refused on private
    and app_only (nobody else reads them) and for a bad instant or a
    window that never shows (400 invalid_show_time — ISO 8601 with a zone).
    The question: "Should posts appear later, or disappear?"
  - RANKABLE NUMBERS — `"rankable": ["score"]` in the collection's file
    names up to 3 number fields (on community, shared and direct each must
    be a declared number field). Then `list({ sort: { by: "score" } })`
    returns the records highest first (`order: "asc"` for lowest first —
    fastest times) and each carries `rank` (1 + how many records the same
    list admits with a better value: ties share, "1, 2, 2, 4"). It ranks
    only what THIS person may already read under the rule, with the same
    `where`, `search`, `count` and `cursor` (rank is within the filter: a
    "this week" where ranks this week); a record with no number in that
    field isn't in a ranked list. Not with `since` (400 invalid_since); a
    field not declared rankable is 400 not_rankable; `sort` takes only
    "newest", "oldest", "updated" or `{ by, order }` (400 invalid_sort).
    A LEADERBOARD's trust comes from who writes the number: keep scores in
    an admin_write or public_read collection (or app_only, read by your
    server) written by your server or a relay after it checked the result —
    never a number each player writes into their own record. Ranking never
    opens a private collection: on private, each person ranks only their
    own. The question: "Do you show a top list ordered by a number — and
    who is trusted to write that number?"
  What the rules canNOT do: there is no team/group/workspace scope and no
  per-user record visibility (records visible to some signed-in users but
  not others). If your app needs that shape, do NOT approximate it by
  filtering a shared collection in the browser — the data still reaches
  every user's device. Stop and tell your human that shape isn't supported
  yet.
  What happens if your human asks for a team or workspace feature (invite
  colleagues, a company account, records shared inside an organisation) →
  tell them Gemmein doesn't support team workspaces, and keep each person's
  data their own (private, or the rule that fits one person); never build
  it from a shared collection plus client-side filtering.
- Record shape: `.create()`/`.get()`/`.update()` return
  `{ id, data: { ...your fields }, createdAt, updatedAt, ownerUserId, ... }` —
  your fields ALWAYS live under `.data` (`record.data.title`, never
  `record.title`). `ownerUserId` and the rest are server-derived and
  read-only: never store your own userId/role/owner fields inside `data`.
  `.list()` returns `{ records, hasMore }` (an object, not an array) and
  accepts `{ limit, sort: "newest"|"oldest"|"updated"|{ by, order }, where,
  search, cursor, since, count, author }` (`{ by }` is a rankable number
  field — see RANKABLE NUMBERS above). limit is 25 by default and 100 at most; a larger ask is refused
  with invalid_limit — page with cursor. `count: true` adds `total` (exact up
  to 10,000) or, past that, `totalAtLeast: 10000` — show "10,000+"; it rides
  the FIRST page only (a `cursor` page carries none — keep the first); it counts
  only what this person could list (never with `since`: 400 invalid_count).
  Never read every record to show a number. `author: "me"` or a
  user id (a record's `ownerUserId`) narrows to one person's records on
  shared, community, public_read and direct ("my posts", "posts by Sam");
  403 author_not_visible on private (already only your own), addressed and
  admin_write. `where: { ownerUserId }` stays refused — `author` is the door. A record's data is at most 32 KB
  (413 payload_too_large); files go through uploads, never inline.
- Filters: `where` on list / watch / count / stats names up to 5 data fields
  (link fields too), all of which must match; a field's value is a literal
  (exact match) or an object of 1..3 operators, all of which must hold —
  `eq` / `ne` (compared as text — `{ eq: "10" }` matches the number 10, as
  a literal always has; null-safe: `{ eq: null }` matches absent or null; a
  bare null literal is refused), `gt` `gte` `lt` `lte` (a number compares
  as a number and a text value in that field never matches; a string
  compares as text in code-unit order, so an ISO date orders correctly),
  `in` / `nin` (a set of 1..50 values), `contains` / `startsWith`
  (case-insensitive text, 1..200 chars; ASCII letters fold), `exists`
  (true / false; absent and null both read as not existing). A relay's `when` and
  `where` read the same grammar (a relay's own cap: 20 fields, 3 operators
  each). `{ amount: { gte: 10 } }`,
  `{ status: { in: ["paid", "sent"] } }`, `{ title: { contains: "invoice" } }`,
  `{ dueAt: { lt: "2026-10-01" } }`. A sealed default is read by eq / ne /
  in / nin; the ordered operators, contains, startsWith and exists read the
  stored value only. Server-managed fields are refused. A `where` outside
  the grammar is 400 invalid_filter, naming the field and the operator.
  Counting and totals, without paging: `g.collection(name).count({ where?,
  search? })` → a number, how many this person could list under the same
  rule, scope and filters; `g.collection(name).stats(field, { where?,
  search? })` → `{ count, sum, avg, min, max }` over the records whose field
  is a number (others skipped; `count` says how many were reduced; the four
  are null when none; a sum past 2^53 is a string). On the wire:
  GET /storage/<collection>/count and /stats?field=; `since`, `sort`,
  `cursor`, `limit` and `expand` are refused there (400 invalid_count /
  400 invalid_stats), and a field name outside the shape's own field grammar
  (a letter, then letters, digits or underscores) is 400 invalid_stats; both doors sit under the list's read limiter and count as
  a read in a secret key's ledger. No `or` group, no sort by a data field;
  `search` is a case-insensitive substring match on the record's values (text
  and numbers, at any depth), never its field names; `stats` reduces one field per call.
  Records — what happens if…:
  - If the collection doesn't exist → 404 unknown_collection: declare it
    in gemmein/collections/<name>.json (gemmein dev picks it up; sync
    carries it to Development; promote carries it to Live — the dashboard's
    Go live page or `npx gemmein go-live`). The app's own calls get one
    neutral sentence (it never says what Development holds); the CLI
    signed in with `npx gemmein login` gets the Development step. Ask your human for the safety rule, never
    guess it.
  - If a community, shared or direct collection's fields aren't declared →
    400 collection_not_declared; a write carrying an undeclared field →
    400 undeclared_field; setting a retired field → 400 field_deprecated.
    Each names the file to change (see Shapes).
  - If someone reads another person's private records → they see none:
    list() returns only their own, get() answers 404.
  - If someone edits or deletes a record they didn't write (shared,
    community) → 404, the same answer as a record that doesn't exist.
  - If a filter runs on a private collection → it narrows the person's own
    records; it never reaches anyone else's.
  - If your code sends id, userId, role or another server-managed field →
    403 forbidden, naming the field. Remove it; the server sets these.
  - If the data is not a plain object → 400 invalid_body.
  - If a record's data is over 32 KB → 413 payload_too_large. Keep large
    content in a file (upload()).
  - If a list asks for more than 100 records, or 0 → 400 invalid_limit,
    never cut down for you; with no limit you get 25, hasMore and a cursor.
    Page with cursor.
  - If a `where` uses an unknown operator or too many fields → 400
    invalid_filter, naming the field and the operator.
  - If one IP (an IPv6 address counts by its /64) writes more than 60 times in a minute → 429 with resetAt
    (reads allow 150 a minute). Wait until resetAt.
  - If a create times out and you retry it without a key → the retry can
    make a second record. Give creates that must happen once a key; the
    retry then returns the first record (existing: true).
  - If a secret key reads or writes outside its collections, or writes
    with a read-only scope → 403 scope_denied. Ask your human to widen
    the key.
  - If a collection that still has records is deleted from the CLI → 409
    collection_not_empty. Delete its records first.
  - If your human deletes it in the dashboard (typing its name) → it goes,
    its records are kept 30 days, and the name can be used again for a
    new, empty collection.
  - If a record is deleted → it is kept 30 days and its files stay. After 30 days it is removed for good, and so are the files
    only it referenced. Files a buyer owns (a product's file, a file an
    access grant or payment names) and files another record still
    references are kept. Nothing to do.
- Live data (dashboards, feeds, inboxes): nothing is pushed — BY DESIGN
  (pushed data is where other platforms leak; every Gemmein read passes the
  permission check). Instead, polling is built in and cheap:

      const w = g.collection("orders").watch(({ records, deleted, initial }) => {
        // initial=true → REPLACE your state with `records` (it IS the full
        // current set — replacing is what clears anything removed while you
        // weren't looking). initial=false → upsert `records` BY ID and drop
        // ids in `deleted`.
      });
      // when the view unmounts: w.stop()

  Every 10s by default (`{ every: ms }`, floor 5s) it asks "what changed?" —
  a near-free answer when nothing did. It sleeps while the tab is hidden and
  refreshes fully on return. Apply records by id: a change can be delivered
  twice, never silently missed. One watch per page, shared — don't stack a
  watcher per component, and never wrap it in your own setInterval. Under
  the hood it's `list({ since })`: pass the previous answer's `watermark` as
  `since` and you get records changed or deleted after it (ids in
  `deleted`), oldest first — same permissions as any read. `since` can't
  combine with `sort`. A record erased by the platform (data erasure, not an
  app delete) doesn't appear in `deleted` — the replace-on-initial refresh
  on tab-return is what clears it. Watching with `where`/`search`: deletions
  always come through, but a record EDITED so it stops matching your filter
  isn't reported (it isn't deleted) — it clears on the next tab-return
  refresh. Watch suits lists you'd actually render (up to a few thousand
  records); it re-reads the full list on every tab return.
- Telling a customer something happened ("order shipped", "booking
  confirmed", "new reply") is built in — your SERVER calls it with a
  secret key; there is no SMTP, no email service to wire, and it cannot
  be called from the browser:

      import { gemmeinServer } from "@gemmein/sdk";
      const g = gemmeinServer(process.env.GEMMEIN_SECRET_KEY);
      await g.notify(order.ownerUserId, {
        subject: "Your order shipped",
        text: "Order #142 left the warehouse today.",
        key: "order-142-shipped",   // retries can't double-send
      });

  A person id, NEVER an email address — the recipient must be a verified
  user of your app (404 not_a_customer otherwise; the address comes from
  the server's own record). Plain text; a short "you have an account with
  {your app}" footer is added for you. notify sends only from YOUR verified
  sender domain: until one is verified on the Domains page the send is
  refused (409 sender_domain_required) — nothing leaves, nothing is
  recorded, no cap is spent, and the same key sends once you verify. If
  your provider refuses that address at send time the call fails
  (502 send_failed) and is safe to retry; it is never quietly re-sent from
  a Gemmein address. Sign-in codes are the one email Gemmein sends on your
  behalf before a domain is verified, as "<App name> (via Gemmein)".
  THREE SENDER WORDS. A verified domain carries three, set on its page in
  the console: `account`, `support` and `news`. Sign-in codes and
  every email to one person leave from the account word — notify of
  either kind, a relay's email_person and Gemmein's own purchase email (the
  kind sets only the cap); the news word is for broadcasts; your own Inbox
  replies from the support word. Each is a real address: a reply to any of them lands in
  your Inbox, labelled by the word it arrived at. Two kinds can never share
  one word; the console refuses it.
  Every send appears in your
  dashboard Inbox as a conversation; a customer's REPLY lands there too
  once your domain's receiving is verified (the Domains page) — before
  that the mail has no reply path, so if you expect answers, say where to
  write. The response's `replyRail: true|false` states which is true right
  now. This is for EVENTS, not campaigns:
  5 event-class sends per person per day (429 notify_capped with
  resetAt says when). Account activity — a new sign-in, an access change,
  a billing problem — passes `kind: "account"`, which skips the per-person
  cap (a security notice never loses to five order emails); misusing it
  for campaigns shows in your own audit trail. DEVELOPMENT IS STRICTLY
  CAPPED: in the cloud's Development environment every send — notify of
  either kind, a relay's email_person, the purchase email — shares 20 a
  day per app and 50 a day per account (429 development_capped, "test
  volume with npx gemmein dev"). Sign-in codes are outside that budget —
  they have their own: 100 sign-in code emails a day per app (test
  members' codes don't count) — and Live has no such budget. Test volume locally. In `gemmein dev` the send
  prints in the terminal (NOTIFY · …) instead of mailing.
  What happens if… (notify; a relay's email_person rides the same caps):
  - If no domain is verified for email → 409 sender_domain_required for a real person; nothing leaves, nothing is recorded, no cap is spent. Verify it on the Domains page; the same key then sends once. A test member in Development needs no domain: the email lands in the test mailbox (`npx gemmein mail`, `test_mail`) and never leaves Gemmein.
  - If the person id is unknown, from another environment, or suspended → 404 not_a_customer; nothing is sent. Use a person id from the key's own environment.
  - If you retry with the same key → one email; the retry answers deduped: true with the first send's id and spends no cap. Nothing to do.
  - If two people get the same key → both are sent; a key is scoped to its person. Nothing to do.
  - If two sends with one key arrive at once → the second answers 409 in_flight; after the first finishes the key answers deduped: true. Retry after a moment.
  - If a person has had 5 event emails today → 429 notify_capped with resetAt; kind: "account" is outside this cap. Wait for resetAt, or send account notices as kind: "account".
  - If the app has sent 200 emails this hour → 429 notify_capped with resetAt, for either kind. Wait for resetAt.
  - If the provider fails or refuses your address → 502 send_failed; nothing is sent from a Gemmein address and the cap is handed back. Retry with the same key.
  - If the owner switched sends off in Emails → 403 sends_disabled on every notify. Don't retry; the owner switches sends back on.
  - If subject, text or person is missing → 400 no_subject, no_text or no_person; a kind other than "event" or "account" is 400 invalid_kind. Fix the call.
  - If the subject contains line breaks → they are removed before sending; a subject cannot add mail headers. Nothing to do.
  - If receiving is not verified → the email is sent with replyRail: false and a reply cannot reach the Inbox. Say in the text where to write.
  - If the person is erased → their sends are removed from the records. Nothing to do.
  - If the person's address hard-bounced, or they marked this app's mail as spam → `200` with `sent: false`, `notSent: "address_bounced"` or `"address_complained"` and a `message` ("not sent: address bounced" / "not sent: address marked as spam"); nothing leaves and no cap is spent. A relay's email_person is skipped with the same sentence. Don't retry; the owner sees a note on the person's page and can turn the person's email back on there.
- Email templates: the emails Gemmein sends for the app can wear the
  founder's own design. Write one HTML file per email in
  gemmein/emails/<name>.html, and the sign-in email's brand in
  gemmein/emails/sign-in.json; `npx gemmein sync` carries them to the
  cloud's Development, go-live and promote copy Development's into Live, and
  `npx gemmein dev` uses the same files exactly as the cloud does (each send
  lands in gemmein/.data/mail). With no file, that email sends in Gemmein's
  plain design. The files, and what each may use:
    sign-in.json    the sign-in code email — a BRAND CONFIG, never HTML:
                    { "logoUrl": "https://…/logo.png", "brandColour": "#0f7a5a",
                      "backgroundColour": "#f2f5f3", "appName": "Coachly",
                      "greeting": "Welcome back to Coachly" }
                    (every key optional). Gemmein renders the whole email in
                    one fixed layout around its own code; the subject and the
                    plain-text part stay Gemmein's.
    purchase.html   {{app_name}} {{product}} {{library_url}}
    plan-start.html {{app_name}} {{plan}} {{trial_end}} {{price_after}}
                    {{account_url}} — a paid plan or its free trial began
                    ({{trial_end}} is empty for a paid start)
    notify.html     {{app_name}} {{subject}} {{body}} — every g.notify() and
                    relay email_person, unless a more specific one exists:
    notify-account.html  the same vars — notify with kind "account"
    notify-event.html    the same vars — notify with kind "event"
    email-person.html    the same vars — a relay's email_person (then
                    notify-<kind>, then notify)
    inbox-reply.html     {{app_name}} {{subject}} {{content}} — the founder's
                    Inbox replies and new conversations; {{content}} (once)
                    is the message
  sign-in.json rules: logoUrl is an https image with no user part — at
  save Gemmein fetches it ONCE (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, 200 KB at most, no
  redirects), keeps its own copy in the app's storage, and the email shows
  that copy, never your URL; changing the image at your URL changes nothing
  until the next save that changes sign-in.json. brandColour and
  backgroundColour are #rrggbb, and a brandColour too light to read the code
  on its tint is refused. With no colour and no logo set (and no email
  accent in the console), the sign-in email and Gemmein's plain design
  follow the reader's light or dark mode; with any of them set, they stay
  light, the background your colour or logo was made for. appName (60 characters) is only the header label
  shown when there is no logo — the sentence beside the code and the logo's
  alt text always name the app by its real name. appName and greeting (120)
  are one line of plain text with no digits or numerals (Roman numerals
  included) and nothing URL-like (a scheme, or a dot followed by a domain
  ending) — invisible and tag characters are removed and fullwidth or styled
  digits normalised before that check; "Hi. Welcome back" is fine.
  An HTML template: write a whole document; tables and inline styles read
  best in mail clients; a <style> block is fine (Gemmein inlines it).
  Allowed: layout and text elements (table, tr, td, div, p, span, h1–h6, a,
  img, b, i, strong, em, ul, ol, li, br, hr, center, font…), their
  presentational attributes, and inline CSS for colour, background-color,
  fonts, spacing, borders, sizes, alignment and display, as plain values.
  Gemmein removes: script, forms and their controls, iframe, object, embed,
  svg, video/audio, <link>, <meta>, <base>, comments (Outlook conditionals
  too), every on…= handler, CSS url()/expression()/@import/@font-face,
  calc()/min()/max()/clamp()/var() and other CSS maths, position,
  transform, z-index, filter and negative values (letter- and word-spacing
  aside). Links are https:, mailto: or #; images are https: only; a URL
  with a user part (https://a@b) is removed. @media rules are kept when
  every selector names a class. Every {{var}} value is HTML-escaped;
  {{body}} and {{content}} keep their line breaks; {{library_url}} is the
  only var that may be a whole href. Gemmein renders the template inside its
  own clipping box and appends its footer AFTER it (the app's name and
  sending domain, and why the person got it), then derives the plain-text
  part. None of these emails is marketing, so none carries an unsubscribe
  line. The cloud keeps a template's last 10 versions.

      npx gemmein emails                  what each email uses, synced or not
      npx gemmein emails preview notify   the LOCAL file with sample data → a file to open; nothing sent
      npx gemmein emails test notify      ONE test of the synced template to your own address
      npx gemmein emails remove notify    back to Gemmein's plain design (delete the file too)

  What happens if… (email templates):
  - If a template uses a {{var}} its email doesn't have → sync refuses that file with 400 unknown_variable, naming the vars it has; the other files still sync. Use only the listed vars.
  - If a file name isn't one of the seven → refused (unknown_template) and never synced. Rename it.
  - If there is a sign-in.html → it is never synced; the sign-in email takes no HTML. Write sign-in.json.
  - If sign-in.json has another key, a greeting or app name with a digit or an address, a colour that isn't #rrggbb or is too light, or a logo that isn't https → 400 invalid_brand with the reason. Fix the value.
  - If the logo can't be fetched at save (not a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, over 200 KB, a redirect, an error, or a private address) → 400 logo_unavailable with the reason; nothing is saved. Fix the address or the image and save again.
  - If a template is over 100 KB → refused (template_too_large). Host images at https addresses and trim the HTML.
  - If a template carries a script, a form, an event handler, CSS maths or an http: image → saved with those removed; sync prints "stripped by Gemmein: …". Nothing to do, or remove them from the file.
  - If inbox-reply.html has no {{content}}, or two → refused (content_slot). Put it in once.
  - If a template is missing, or can't be read or rendered when an email sends → that email goes out in Gemmein's plain design. Nothing is lost.
  - If you save a template on Live → 409 templates_live_refused. Save it in Development; go-live or promote copies it into Live.
  - If an app saves templates 60 times in an hour, or previews them 120 times → 429 templates_capped with resetAt (150 saves and 300 previews an hour per account). Preview locally with `npx gemmein emails preview`, which is never capped.
  - If you send a test → one email, subject "[Test] …", to the address you're signed in with, never anyone else. It counts toward Development's 20 a day per app and 50 per account; past that, 429 development_capped.
  - If a file is deleted from gemmein/emails/ → the cloud keeps the template; `npx gemmein emails remove <name>` takes it down. In `npx gemmein dev` the deleted file's template is removed at once.
- Your compute, Gemmein's gate: when code of yours must run elsewhere (a model
  call, a PDF render, a nightly job), that function is your own server
  code, running on your own host, anywhere — and it asks Gemmein its only
  three questions: who is this person, what do they hold, change what
  they hold.

      import { gemmeinServer } from "@gemmein/sdk";
      const g = gemmeinServer(process.env.GEMMEIN_SECRET_KEY);
      const { person, holdings } = await g.verifySession(token);
      if (!holdings.access.includes("access:pro")) return deny();
      await g.holdings(personId);                    // no token in hand
      await g.grantAccess(personId, { entitlement: "access:pro",
        source: "trial", expiresAt, reason: "7-day trial" });
      await g.revokeAccess(personId, grantId, { reason: "trial ended" });
      const { person, created } = await g.invitePerson("client@example.com");

  A secret key with the capability may create a person by email BEFORE
  they sign in — the envelope, the invoice, the client portal, the
  booking-winner email: create the person, hand them the file, address
  the record, notify them; their first sign-in lands on a ready account.
  `invitePerson(email)` is create-or-fetch (created: true the first time,
  false after; one id, case-insensitive) and is the ONE server call that
  takes an email; everything else takes the person id it returns. The
  owner sees them as "invited · hasn't signed in yet" until they sign in.
  ONE verifySession per request answers identity AND holdings — don't
  call it twice, don't cache the answer past the request. `holdings` is
  what the person holds NOW: `access` (keys like "access:pro"), `grants`
  (each with its source KIND only — subscription | purchase | manual |
  trial | promotion | migration | relay — plus start and expiry), and `credits`,
  `{ balance, reserved, expiring }` — the meter: spendable now, held by
  runs in flight, the soonest credits that will die or null (engine 0.12.0;
  `{ balance }` alone from 0.8.0; `null` from an older local engine). Never subscription status, amounts
  or Stripe ids: gate on what a person HOLDS, never on billing. Person
  id, NEVER an email address. verifySession needs nothing extra; looking
  someone up by id and granting are new power, so they sit behind per-key
  checkboxes the HUMAN ticks when minting the key — ask your human to
  tick "Look up a person's access by id" / "Grant and revoke access" /
  "Create a person by email before they sign in" (invitePerson) /
  "Spend a person's credits" (spendCredits). A
  key grants MANUAL access only (manual | trial | promotion | migration):
  purchases and subscriptions come from the built-in Stripe path, and
  another provider's payment grants through a relay (source `relay`). Every /server/*
  call a resolved secret key makes, ok or refused, lands in that key's
  usage ledger on the owner's API keys page (a rejected or publishable key
  can't be attributed, so it reaches only the request log); refusals also
  write one activity row per key, route and code each hour. A key's reach
  is the collections it is scoped to, what it may do with people, or both —
  a people-only key (no collection) is a normal key; only a key that
  reaches nothing is refused at mint. In `gemmein
  dev` the local key already holds both capabilities, and the usage read
  is cloud-only — the local runtime never mounts the console. The
  refusals, and what to do:
      session_invalid     no session matches this token — the person must
                          sign in again; never reuse tokens across people
      session_expired     the session ended — back to sign-in
      session_revoked     signed out on one of their devices, or by the
                          owner — sign-in
      person_suspended    the owner suspended them — access is off until
                          the owner reactivates them in the dashboard
      person_not_found    no person with this id in this app and env —
                          ids come from verifySession or the dashboard
      capability_required the box isn't ticked on this key — ask your
                          human to mint one with it ticked
      unknown_plan        no plan or product by that name — declare it
                          in gemmein/payments.json; sync sets it
      grant_not_found     not this person's grant here — re-read holdings
      already_revoked     a grant ends once — it is already ended
      invalid_source      purchase/subscription asked for by hand — use
                          manual | trial | promotion | migration instead
      invalid_id          a prototype name (__proto__, constructor) was
                          sent as a person or grant id — ids come from
                          verifySession or the dashboard, never a name
      invalid_body        one malformed field (token, expiresAt, reason)
                          — the message names which one and what it needs
      invalid_email       invitePerson: must look like name@domain
      invite_capped       invitePerson: 500 invite calls per app per day (a
                          fetch of an existing person counts) — the message
                          says where to write; resetAt says when
- Relays — Gemmein runs them: receives the event, maps the fields, carries
  out the action.
  What it is: a rule in one JSON file — when this happens, Gemmein does
  these things, keeps a row per event, retries, and shows every run in the
  owner's dashboard with a replay button. A relay takes a verified signal
  and closes a circuit: GoCardless says paid, the relay opens access,
  writes the receipt, tells the person, passes the signal to your URL.
  Stripe stays built in; any provider that signs its webhooks drives
  access the same way.
  What happens if…
  - When: in Live, a receiver, data_change, run_started or credits_low
    relay runs within seconds of its event; a receiver answers the
    provider first, then runs it. A schedule runs on its tick. In
    Development, relays run immediately, 1 run per app at a time, up to
    120 immediate relay runs per app and 300 per account an hour; past that, events wait
    their turn and run within minutes — never dropped. For volume, run on
    `npx gemmein dev`.
  - Payment relays: a relay with an action that grants or takes what a
    person holds (grant_access, revoke_access, grant_credits,
    fulfil_product, refund_product, grant_plan, revoke_plan) is a payment
    relay — including one that also has start_run. Payment events from
    your provider (receiver relays) for one customer run in the order the
    payments happened, across all payment relays: the mapped `paid_at` (a
    time later than the event's arrival counts as its arrival), else when
    the event arrived. A payment relay's event runs 2 seconds after it
    arrives, so an event sent a moment earlier lands first.
  - A refund waits for its payment: while the same customer's earlier
    payment event is queued, running or retrying, the refund waits; it
    runs once the payment succeeds or is dead.
  - Other relays, and the other kinds (record changes, run starts,
    credits running low), run in order only within themselves: one
    record's changes, or one person's events, on that relay. They never
    wait for another relay.
  - A paused payment relay holds that customer's later events on payment
    relays. After 60 seconds a Problem names the relay they wait on
    ("Refund" waits: relay "Paid" is paused); resume it and they run.
  - AI runs: a relay with start_run and no grant or take action never
    waits for a payment relay and never holds one; it runs in order within
    itself. A relay with start_run plus any grant or take action is a
    payment relay.
  - Editing a relay while an event waits to retry: a retry runs the relay
    as it is now. A grant or take already done for that event is never
    repeated. Changing which product or access a grant gives counts as a
    new grant; changing a plan or credit amount applies to new events
    only. call_url can receive the event again — deduplicate on its `id`.
  - Without an edit, a retry skips the steps that already succeeded and
    continues from the one that failed. A replay runs every step again.
  - Adding or removing a grant or take action makes a relay a payment
    relay or not; events already waiting follow the change when it is
    saved.
  - Deploys and restarts: unfinished runs go back to the queue and
    finished steps do not repeat. A call_url that was in flight can
    arrive twice — deduplicate on its `id`.
  - `paid_at`: map it whenever the provider sends a payment time. Without
    it, a payment for an address whose owner deleted their account grants
    nothing, and it shows on the Errors page.
  - Failures: a failed run retries after 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 8 h
    and 16 h, then is dead — the owner is alerted and can replay it.
  - Waiting shows on the Errors page, never dropped: relays_delayed (Live
    only: a relay's events waited over 30 s; kept, run in order) · relays_held (an
    event waited over 60 s behind an earlier event for the same record or
    person — the sentence names the relay it waits behind and why: resume
    or fix that one) · relays_dev_capped (Development passed 120 immediate
    relay runs an app, 300 an account, in an hour; the rest run within minutes — for
    volume use npx gemmein dev).
  Does: write a record · grant access · revoke access · grant credits ·
  fulfil or refund a product · grant or revoke a plan · email the person the
  event is about · call your URL (a signed notice to a server YOU run) ·
  start a run on a named AI tool for the event's person (start_run —
  credits held from them; a tool on provider external still submits
  itself straight to its own URL, no relay row involved — see the AI card).
  Does not: run your code; call OpenAI or any third API for you (call_url
  carries Gemmein's body and signature, never your key or a request you
  shape); attach a person to a schedule (no "email everyone due tomorrow"
  yet); transform data with custom logic; act on more than one person per event
  (a list is a broadcast); spend credits (a spend is your server's or the
  AI route's — a relay only adds).
  Needs something else when: the work THINKS — a model call, a score, a
  transform, a third API — put that in your own function behind call_url;
  it receives a verified event with the person already resolved. The AI
  route is where Gemmein holds your provider key and makes a chat call for
  a signed-in person at the tool's credit price (one by default) — see
  The AI route.
  Use a relay when: a provider other than Stripe signs a webhook that
  should change access or write a record (GoCardless, Paddle, Lemon
  Squeezy, a form or signature tool); a record change should tell the
  person or open access; something should run on a clock and write a
  record or ping your URL.
  Not when: the work needs custom transforms or reshaping (that is your function);
  one event should email many people (a relay addresses one person); a schedule
  must address a person (not yet); you already use Stripe for the money —
  the built-in Stripe path already grants access and writes receipts, and
  a relay adds nothing there.
  The GoCardless case end to end — a payment confirms, the payer gets Pro,
  an email, and your function hears about it. The file is
  `gemmein/relays/<name>.json`; the owner's dashboard (the Relays room)
  creates and edits it too, pauses, resumes, rotates and deletes it, and
  shows where it came from ("from file, synced <when>" / "edited here
  <when>"), its receiver URL, its secrets (minted ones shown once there;
  the ones sync mints are saved in gemmein/.data/secrets.json), every event with
  each action's result, and a replay button:

      {
        "name": "gocardless-paid",
        "trigger": {
          "kind": "receiver",
          "verify": { "scheme": "signature", "header": "Webhook-Signature" },
          "map": {
            "event_id": "events.0.id",
            "event_type": "events.0.action",
            "person_email": "events.0.details.customer_email"
          },
          "when": { "event_type": "confirmed" }
        },
        "actions": [
          { "type": "grant_access", "entitlement": "Pro", "reason": "GoCardless payment {{mapped.event_id}}" },
          { "type": "email_person", "subject": "Your payment is confirmed", "text": "Thanks. Pro is open on your account." },
          { "type": "call_url", "url": "https://hooks.example.com/paid" }
        ]
      }

  Triggers (exactly one per relay):
  - receiver — a provider's signed webhook at `POST /hooks/<appId>/<name>`;
    `verify` names the scheme (signature | stripe | svix |
    shared_token), `map` names dotted paths into the body (`event_id`
    dedupes, ONE person key resolves the person, the rest ride as
    `{{mapped.<name>}}`), `when` filters mapped fields — per field a literal
    (exact match) or an object of operators, the list's own filter grammar.
    A map names the person ONE way: person_email (their address, which
    invites someone who has never signed in), person_id (a gemmein person
    id) or person_token (the store account token their app filed with a
    store). Two of them in one map is refused at save — the id and the
    token could name different people, and the event would land on
    whichever was tried first. Only `person_email` creates a person;
    `person_id` and `person_token` are read-only lookups, because a value a
    third party chose that matches nothing names no human at all. A key
    that resolves to nobody records the event, answers 200 and reports
    `person_not_found` naming the KEY that was tried, never its value.
    OPTIONAL `paid_at` — the provider's payment-time field (unix seconds,
    milliseconds or an ISO date; a time later than the event's arrival
    counts as its arrival). WHENEVER the provider's event carries a payment
    time, map it as `paid_at` on any relay that grants (access, credits, a
    product or a plan): a
    person who deleted their account is a NEW customer only for a payment
    dated after the deletion. Without `paid_at`, a payment for a deleted
    address invites no one and grants nothing — it is a Problem for your
    human to refund or grant by hand.
    RECEIVERS ARE STANDARDS, NOT PROVIDERS. Any sender that signs its
    webhooks by a standard mechanism works — there is no list of allowed
    providers. Read the SENDER'S OWN webhook docs and answer four questions:
    which algorithm, which key, what text is signed, where the signature is.
    - `signature` — THE SIGNATURE RECIPE. Every field is optional
      except where the signature is; left out, it is the plain case (an
      HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body, hex, in one header):
      · which algorithm → `algorithm`: `hmac-sha256` (default), `hmac-sha1`,
        `hmac-sha512` (a shared secret), or `ed25519`, `ecdsa-p256-sha256`
        (the sender signs with its private key and publishes the PUBLIC
        key — that public key is what you store; Gemmein never makes one).
      · where the signature is → `header` (a header of its own), or
        `signatureField`, a dotted path inside the JSON (or form) body,
        like `signature.signature`. Exactly one.
      · the header carries parts like `h1=…`, `v1=…`, `v0=…`, `sha256=…`
        → `signatureKey` names the part that is the signature (several of
        that name: any one matching is enough — a secret rotation); parts
        separated by `;` (`ts=…;h1=…`) → `"separator": ";"` (default `,`).
      · where the timestamp is → `timestampHeader` (a header of its own),
        `timestampKey` (a part inside the signature header, like `ts=`) or
        `timestampField` (a path in the body). One at most. With one, a
        replay window applies (`toleranceSeconds` 1..300, default 300).
      · what text is signed → `signedPayload`, a template (≤ 40 characters,
        letters, digits and . : _ - around the placeholders):
        `{timestamp}`; `{url}` — the receiver URL exactly as the relay's page
        shows it (the engine's configured public address, never the Host
        header; a call with anything after it, a `?query` included, never
        verifies); and ONE that ends the text: `{body}` (the raw body),
        `{params}` (a form post's fields sorted by name, each name then
        value — only for application/x-www-form-urlencoded) or `{token}`
        (a body value named by `tokenField`, beside a body signature).
        Default: `{timestamp}.{body}` with a timestamp, `{body}` without.
      · how it is spelt → `encoding`: `hex` (default), `base64`, `base64url`.
      Example recipes, each proven against the sender's published spec
      (ops/relays/verified-senders.json — a sender is named here only while
      its test passes):
        GitHub      { "scheme": "signature", "header": "X-Hub-Signature-256", "signatureKey": "sha256" }
        GoCardless  { "scheme": "signature", "header": "Webhook-Signature" }
        Lemon Squeezy  { "scheme": "signature", "header": "X-Signature" }
        Shopify     { "scheme": "signature", "header": "X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256", "encoding": "base64" }
        Paddle      { "scheme": "signature", "header": "Paddle-Signature", "timestampKey": "ts", "signatureKey": "h1", "separator": ";", "signedPayload": "{timestamp}:{body}" }
        Slack       { "scheme": "signature", "header": "X-Slack-Signature", "timestampHeader": "X-Slack-Request-Timestamp", "signatureKey": "v0", "signedPayload": "v0:{timestamp}:{body}" }
        Intercom    { "scheme": "signature", "algorithm": "hmac-sha1", "header": "X-Hub-Signature", "signatureKey": "sha1" }
        Square      { "scheme": "signature", "header": "x-square-hmacsha256-signature", "encoding": "base64", "signedPayload": "{url}{body}" }
        Twilio      { "scheme": "signature", "algorithm": "hmac-sha1", "header": "X-Twilio-Signature", "encoding": "base64", "signedPayload": "{url}{params}" }
        Mailgun     { "scheme": "signature", "signatureField": "signature.signature", "timestampField": "signature.timestamp", "tokenField": "signature.token", "signedPayload": "{timestamp}{token}" }
        SendGrid    { "scheme": "signature", "algorithm": "ecdsa-p256-sha256", "header": "X-Twilio-Email-Event-Webhook-Signature", "timestampHeader": "X-Twilio-Email-Event-Webhook-Timestamp", "encoding": "base64", "signedPayload": "{timestamp}{body}" }
        Discord     { "scheme": "signature", "algorithm": "ed25519", "header": "X-Signature-Ed25519", "timestampHeader": "X-Signature-Timestamp", "signedPayload": "{timestamp}{body}" }
      EVENTS ARE KEPT 30 DAYS after they finish (done, dead or failed —
      queued and running ones are never removed), then deleted, nightly in
      the cloud and by `gemmein dev`'s own sweep; a deleted relay's
      single-use record goes 24 hours after the delete. Dedupe lives on
      those rows, so for a sender that signs no timestamp (GitHub,
      Intercom, Square, Twilio) a call captured more than 30 days ago
      could run once more — its signature has no age to refuse it by.
      A form post (Twilio's) is read as its fields: map them by name
      (`"event_id": "MessageSid"`). Where the sender signs no timestamp
      (GitHub, Intercom, Square, Twilio…), a resent event is deduped by its
      `event_id` (else by the body, within the UTC day) — there is no replay
      window to apply.
      WHAT A SIGNATURE THAT IS NOT OVER THE RAW BODY PROVES — read this
      before a `{token}` or `{params}` relay grants anything:
      · `{token}` (Mailgun): the signature covers the timestamp and token
        only. The event itself (`event-data`) is NOT authenticated: anyone
        who captures one signed call can send it to this relay with ANY
        body, once, within 5 minutes of its timestamp. Mailgun signs every
        webhook of an account with ONE key, and the URL is not signed, so a
        call captured from any of your Mailgun webhooks — another URL,
        another relay of yours using that key — serves.
      · `{params}` (Twilio): the fields are joined name+value with nothing
        between them, so one signed call can be re-split into other fields
        under the same signature (`Body=hi&Sid=S1` and `Bodyh=iSidS1` sign
        the same text). The URL is signed, so a capture serves only here.
      Gemmein accepts each such signature ONCE — the event is keyed by its
      signed text, still for 24 hours after the relay is deleted (re-made
      under its name, it refuses a used one) — so a capture and its
      re-split never both run: whichever arrives first is recorded. Treat
      such an event's fields as the sender's claim.
      UNSIGNED EVENTS — ONE RULE: a receiver whose sender doesn't sign
      the event itself — a `{token}` recipe (Mailgun), or `shared_token`
      (the same token on every call: whoever captures it can send any
      number of fake events, at any time) — only writes records and calls
      your URL by default. Every other action (grant_access, grant_credits,
      grant_plan, fulfil_product, start_run, revoke_access, revoke_plan,
      refund_product, email_person) answers 400 `invalid_definition`
      ("actions[i] <type>: this sender doesn't sign the event itself — …
      Anyone who captures one call can fake one event within 5 minutes
      [a shared token: fake any number of events at any time]. To let this
      relay act on it anyway, set trigger.trustUnsignedEvents: true; or
      keep this relay to write_record and call_url, have your function
      check the event with the sender's API, and act from a
      data_change."). So does a map naming `person_email` (it creates
      people): name the person by `person_id` or `person_token`, which
      never create anyone. The same refusal holds in `gemmein dev`,
      `gemmein sync`, the dashboard and Promote (its dry run names the
      relay as not carried). A record a relay writes never fires a
      data_change relay, so write_record cannot be turned into a grant.
      `{params}` (Twilio), `{body}` recipes, stripe and svix sign the event
      and need nothing. The safer way to act on Mailgun or a shared-token
      sender: call_url to your function, which checks the event with the
      sender's API and writes a record with your secret key; a data_change
      relay on that collection acts.
      THE OPT-IN, `"trigger": { …, "trustUnsignedEvents": true }`: the
      relay acts on events its sender doesn't sign. NEVER set it without
      asking the human first, and ask in plain words: "this sender proves
      a message came from it (or only that the caller knows a token), but
      not what the message says — someone who sees one real message can
      send fake ones, and this relay would grant, take away, email or
      create people from them." On save, `gemmein sync` / `gemmein dev`
      print the one-line warning once, the relay's page shows it beside
      the setting, Logs carries the change (trustUnsignedEvents before →
      after, who did it), and Promote carries it to Live with the warning
      in the dry run. It is refused on a sender that signs the event
      ("…remove it") and when it is not true or false. With it on, a save
      that WIDENS what a captured call buys (a longer toleranceSeconds, no
      timestamp, or a move to shared_token) answers the warning again;
      Logs records every such change (forgeryWindow before → after). A
      relay stored without it that breaks the rule refuses every event
      (401 `bad_signature`) and raises the Problem `relay_unsigned_event`.
      An event that arrived unsigned never acts later either: if the relay
      changed to act without the opt-in before it ran, it ends dead
      ("…nothing ran"), and replaying it answers 409 `unsigned_event`. The
      go-live and Promote previews name each opted-in relay with its
      warning, and each relay they will not copy with why.
      What happens if… the save names an unknown placeholder (`{ts}`),
      ends with anything but one of `{body}`, `{params}`, `{token}`, names
      a placeholder twice, puts a digit or `{params}` right after
      `{timestamp}` (a timestamp is digits — the next character never is;
      `{timestamp}{body}` is fine, a body opening with a digit never
      verifies), leaves `{timestamp}` out while a timestamp is named (a
      timestamp the signature does not cover proves nothing), names
      `{timestamp}` or `{token}` with no source, puts `{body}`/`{params}`
      in the text while the signature itself is in the body, names two
      timestamp sources or both `header` and `signatureField`, an unknown
      `algorithm`, or a separator other than `,` or `;`: 400
      `invalid_definition`, the message saying which and how to fix it;
      nothing saved. A timestamp that is not 1–13 digits never verifies.
      The definition saves but describes the signature differently from how
      the sender signs (e.g. Paddle with the default `.` join, another
      algorithm, or a receiver URL registered with a query string): every
      event answers 401 `bad_signature` and nothing runs — compare the
      verify block with the sender's docs. A header listing more than 8
      signatures: 400 `too_many_signatures` (a sender lists one, or two or
      three while it rotates). A relay stored before the scheme was renamed
      (`hmac_sha256_header`): every event answers 401 `scheme_renamed` —
      save its definition again with `"scheme": "signature"`; a definition
      naming the old scheme is refused at save, naming the new one.
    - `svix` — Standard Webhooks (svix): `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`,
      `webhook-signature` (or the same three as `svix-*`), a `whsec_…`
      secret. Clerk and Resend send Standard Webhooks.
    - `stripe` — Stripe's signature format (`Stripe-Signature: t=…,v1=…`).
    - `shared_token` — a token the sender repeats in a header or query
      (RevenueCat repeats the Authorization value you set).
    THE RECEIVER SECRET — WHOSE IT IS, per relay, on every scheme:
    "Gemmein makes it" — minted (`rcv_…`; on svix a Standard Webhooks
    `whsec_…`), shown once / saved to gemmein/.data/secrets.json for you;
    your human gives it to the sender (a sender that lets you SET the
    secret). Or "the sender gave me one" — pasted on the relay's page
    ("Paste the sender's signing secret…") or piped in: `printf '%s'
    "$SECRET" | npx gemmein relays secret <name>` (stdin only — never an
    argument; Development only; `--local` stores it on the `gemmein dev`
    runtime, e.g. `stripe listen`'s whsec); at least 24 characters, never
    echoed or printed. A pasted value is cleaned (Unicode-normalised, ends
    trimmed) and must be plain ASCII with nothing invisible inside, long and
    not one pattern repeated (nor nearly repeated, counting, or a straight
    or keyboard-row run: 123456…, abcdef…, qwerty…), mixing at least 8
    different characters (6 for digits only or hex; 5 for digits only under 32); a Standard Webhooks (svix) secret starts whsec_
    and its key bytes are long and not one pattern repeated; a 22–23
    character value is taken when it mixes upper- and lower-case letters
    and digits (a base64-spelt key, like Square's). A PUBLIC KEY (an
    `ed25519` or `ecdsa-p256-sha256` recipe) is pasted the same way, as the
    sender shows it — hex, base64 or a PEM block, of the raw key or its
    SubjectPublicKeyInfo — read as a key of that algorithm and stored in one
    spelling (its change is on Logs by fingerprint — the first 8 bytes of
    the SHA-256 of the key — never the key). A key is never a secret: on
    an HMAC recipe, a pasted PEM block or DER key (base64 like MCow…,
    MFkw…, MIIB…, or hex) is refused with "this looks like a public key —
    set the recipe's algorithm to ed25519 or ecdsa-p256-sha256"; a RAW key
    in hex (Discord's 64 hex characters) has no structure to tell it from a
    hex secret, so set the algorithm BEFORE pasting. Moving a recipe between
    a public key and a secret ALWAYS clears the stored value (save, `gemmein
    dev`, Promote) in the same write as the recipe, whatever it is; a
    paste racing a recipe change answers 409 `version_conflict` and stores
    nothing; and an HMAC recipe that holds a key anyway refuses every
    event and raises the Problem `relay_key_as_secret` ("this relay's
    stored value is a public key; paste the sender's signing secret"). A
    raw P-256 point, a JWK, or a DER key with bytes around it is refused
    as a secret too. A private key, a key of another algorithm or curve, or
    anything that is not a key: 400 `invalid_input` saying which; asking
    Gemmein to make one: 400 `provider_secret_required`. Where the
    sender lets you set the secret, prefer letting Gemmein make it. Changing a relay's
    scheme keeps its secret only if the new scheme would accept it — else
    the save clears it and says so (set it again). Promote runs the same
    check on Live: a ticked relay whose Live secret the new scheme refuses
    has it cleared and waits paused for the sender's — the dry run and the
    approval say so first, and Logs records "cleared" — a recipe moving
    between a secret and a public key is such a change. The signature and shared_token schemes start with
    Gemmein's (shown at create); stripe, svix and the public-key recipes
    start with NOTHING (their senders show their own — add the receiver URL
    as an endpoint there, then paste). What happens if… no secret is stored yet: every event
    answers 401 `bad_signature`; you ask Gemmein to make one on a stripe
    relay: 400 `provider_secret_required` (the stripe format's sender
    always generates the secret); you paste under 24 characters, a repeated
    pattern, a run or a placeholder: 400 `invalid_input`, ending "paste
    the full secret from the sender's dashboard, or let Gemmein make one";
    one key already on the same-named relay in the other environment (in
    any spelling): 400 `invalid_input`; a stripe value that
    doesn't start `whsec_` (an API key pasted by mistake), or a svix value
    that isn't whsec_ + base64 of 24–64 bytes: 400 `invalid_input`; the
    project isn't linked to the cloud yet: refused, naming how to link it
    (nothing is read as an answer to a prompt);
    the CLI reads nothing on stdin: nothing is stored, exit 1; you run it
    with `--live`: refused (the CLI stores it in Development only) — in
    Live your human pastes it on the relay's page; the Live push key
    (`sync --live`) tries it: 403
    `scope_denied`. Storing a secret replaces the current one at once and
    is a Logs row (`relay_secret_rotate`, provided: true) — the value is
    never logged or shown again.
  - schedule — `every` 15m | 30m | 1h | 6h | 12h | 1d | 1w, `at: "HH:MM"` UTC
    with 1d or 1w (00:00 when unset); 1w needs `on`, the weekday
    ("monday" … "sunday", lowercase) — a weekly digest is ONE relay:
    { "kind": "schedule", "every": "1w", "on": "monday", "at": "09:00" },
    no "skip the other days" code in your app. One tick per period; no
    person, so person actions are refused. Changing the trigger (its day,
    time or period) never fires it at once — the first tick is the new
    schedule's next boundary. If `on` is missing on 1w, or
    set on any other period, or not a weekday → refused at save with the
    sentence (sync and gemmein dev alike).
  - data_change — `collection`, `on` ⊆ created | updated | deleted, optional
    `where` on the record's data (a literal or an object of operators per
    field, the list's own filter grammar); never for the runner's own writes.
    Authorise on fields the signed-in user cannot set, or from a receiver.
    Optional `published`: false = only drafts (on a collection whose posts
    wait for approval, "a post is waiting"), true = only once public;
    absent = both. A separate key, never inside `where`. Optional
    `openField` (one of the collection's open fields; needs "updated" in
    `on`) fires only when a reader changes that field, with `direction`
    "added" · "taken back" · "set" to narrow it; such a trigger never fires
    on content edits, and one without it never fires on open fields.
  - credits_low — `below` (1..1,000,000,000); fires once each time a
    person's spendable credits fall from `below` or more to under it (a
    spend, a clawback, an expiry, a reservation), never on a rise; the
    person is the event's person; `{{event.balance}}`, `{{event.before}}`,
    `{{event.below}}`. A grant_credits action here refills on every crossing.
  - run_started — `tool?` (any tool's name; absent, every tool); react-only:
    fires once when a person starts a run on it, whatever its provider — a
    run submits itself, so no hand-off action is required or allowed beside
    it; the person is the run's person; `{{event.run.id}}`,
    `{{event.run.tool}}`; one row per run per relay, ever.
  Actions (1 to 10, run in order, each idempotent per event). A relay
  grants or takes each target once: one fulfil_product / refund_product
  per product, one grant_access / revoke_access per access key, one
  grant_plan and one revoke_plan, one grant_credits (write one with the
  summed amount). A second on the same target is refused at save with
  `duplicate_grant_target`, naming the action and its target:
  - write_record { collection, data, to?: "person" } — keyed per event.
  - grant_access { entitlement, expiresAt?, reason? } — source `relay`, the
    seventh grant source; "granted by relay <name>" on the person's page.
  - revoke_access { entitlement } — ends every live grant of it.
  - grant_credits { amount (1..10,000), reason?, expiresInDays? (1..3650), ref? } —
    adds a promotional grant (free, the first to burn) to the person's
    balance, once per event; with expiresInDays what is left dies that
    many days after it lands; the ledger line reads "relay: <reason>".
    With `ref` (a literal like "first-bonus", or a template such as
    "{{event.campaign}}") it is once per person + ref, FOREVER — a second
    event, another relay carrying the same ref, or a renewal a year later
    adds nothing and the run says "already granted to this person under
    ref …". A template ref that names nothing on the event grants nothing
    ("ref … named nothing on this event"). A bonus on a member's first
    payment needs no relay at all: `welcomeBonus` on the plan or product.
  - email_person { subject, text, kind? } — rides notify's caps, and notify's
    sender law: it goes only from your verified sender domain, wearing that
    domain's account word (kind only sets the cap class). Until one is
    verified the action alone is refused sender_domain_required and the event
    records it; nothing is sent via Gemmein. To a TEST MEMBER in Development
    it needs no domain: the email lands in the test mailbox, like their codes.
  - call_url { url } — https, signed POST (`X-Gemmein-Signature`), 10 s; the
    same `id` on every retry and replay — your URL deduplicates on it.
  - start_run { tool, inputs? } — starts a run on `tool` for the EVENT's
    person, the same door POST /ai/run/<tool> reaches; credits held from
    them, never the relay; inputs are the tool's own declared names,
    templated. Not a hand-off — the run submits itself. This is a tool —
    a pipeline included — starting for that person with nobody pressing a
    button: a saved record, a payment, a clock or a webhook fires it. A
    refusal from the run door (unknown_tool, entitlement_required,
    credits_exhausted, …) is a definition-level fact, never retried.
  - fulfil_product { product, ref? } — product is a name on the Payments
    page; ref is the provider's payment reference.
  - refund_product { product, ref? } — the refund twin.
  - grant_plan { plan, ref? } — plan is a name on the Payments page; ref is
    the provider's payment reference. Writes the person's subscription on
    that plan (active, until revoked), grants the plan's key, records the
    payment — the steps a Stripe invoice takes.
  - revoke_plan { plan, ref? } — ends a relay-granted subscription: the
    person lands on the default plan and the plan's key is revoked.
  fulfil_product grants the product's key and credits to the event's
  person and writes the receipt, exactly as a Stripe purchase does;
  refund_product takes them back. Both are idempotent on ref: a ref must
  be the provider's unique payment identifier; a ref already used by
  another purchase is refused and audited. A ref you wrote that names
  nothing on the event is refused, never replaced: only an absent ref
  falls back to rly:<eventId>. The relay road binds by name for
  FULFILMENT: renaming or deleting the relay stops fulfilment until a
  relay with that name exists again; the product card shows it.
  refund_product may run from any relay in the environment; it refunds
  only a purchase a relay fulfilled, for the event's person and the
  product it names. grant_plan is the plan twin (W9.7): it runs only for a
  plan whose "How it's sold" names this relay, is idempotent on ref, and a
  renewal is a new ref that keeps the plan active — there is no lapse
  timer; the provider's END-of-access webhook is the revoke (the
  subscription expired, its period ended, or it was refunded), never its
  "will not renew" cancellation, which would end a paid period early. revoke_plan
  may run from any relay; it ends only a subscription a relay granted (a
  Stripe-billed one is Stripe's to end, said on the event row), lands the
  person on the default plan and revokes exactly the key grant_plan gave.
  One active plan per person: granting another plan is a switch. This is how
  a product sold via a relay (How it's sold = a relay's name, not a
  Stripe Payment Link) gets fulfilled — a provider without Payment Links
  (GoCardless, Lemon Squeezy, Paddle, bank transfer) confirms a payment,
  the relay fulfils the product:

      {
        "name": "gocardless-paid",
        "trigger": {
          "kind": "receiver",
          "verify": { "scheme": "signature", "header": "Webhook-Signature" },
          "map": {
            "event_id": "events.0.id",
            "event_type": "events.0.action",
            "person_email": "events.0.details.customer_email",
            "payment_id": "events.0.links.payment"
          },
          "when": { "event_type": "confirmed" }
        },
        "actions": [
          { "type": "fulfil_product", "product": "Starter pack", "ref": "{{mapped.payment_id}}" }
        ]
      }

  Mapped fields ride into templates as {{mapped.<name>}}; {{event.<path>}}
  reads the raw payload.
  A template that names nothing is recorded as a warning on the relay
  event — read it on the Relays page before trusting a ref.

  YOUR OWN PIPELINE (provider external, DECISION-PIPELINE-PROVIDER 18 Sep
  2026) — a tool on provider external names a URL and runs on it as a
  PROVIDER: starting a run makes the runner POST it straight to that URL,
  signed, on its own retry ladder, exactly as a job goes to Replicate. NO
  RELAY ROW EXISTS FOR A PIPELINE, EVER. Set-up: `url` (https; loopback
  http only on the local rail) and a signing secret (aisk_…, minted on
  create and saved for you in gemmein/.data/secrets.json — never printed;
  rotatable on the tool's page); no url = 409 tool_incomplete before any
  credit moves; bounds.deadlineMinutes (1..1440, default 60) is how long a
  run may take. The hand-off, signed as call_url is:
      { "run": { "id", "tool", "kind", "units", "reserved", "createdAt" },
        "params": { … }, "person": { "id", "email" }, "deadline": "…",
        "complete": { "url": "…/complete", "token": "…", "expiresAt": "…" },
        "progress": { "url": "…/progress" }, "fail": { "url": "…/fail" } }
  A 2xx = acknowledged: the run is running. A non-2xx, timeout or no
  connection rides the ladder with the same body — dedupe on run.id; a 4xx
  other than 408/429 is terminal (failed, hold released). A sealed file
  input arrives as a link that lives five minutes. Your pipeline calls,
  with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (no session; 120 calls a minute):
  - POST …/complete { units?, files?: [{ url, contentType? }], text?,
    data? } — up to 64 KB, up to 10 files (public https URLs copied into
    the person's sealed files — LOCAL RAIL ONLY: also http on localhost /
    127.0.0.1, so your own pipeline running beside gemmein dev can hand back
    a file it serves; the cloud takes https only, through the egress
    guard), text up to 200,000 chars, data returned
    exactly as sent; units settled at the tool's rate, never above the
    hold (absent: the hold charged). 200 { run } succeeded; a result the
    engine could not store: 422 result_refused, failed, hold returned.
  - POST …/fail { error? } (up to 2,000) — 200 { run }, failed.
  - POST …/progress { progress: 0..100, note?: ≤200 } — OPTIONAL, same
    token, non-spending, any number of times, never takes the lease.
    200 { run }; run_ended once the run has ended.
  Refusals: token_required (401) · token_invalid (401 — also for a run
  id that doesn't exist) · run_ended (409 — the token is single use) · run_busy (409 — a
  completion is already in progress; wait, up to five minutes) ·
  not_external (409 — a Gemmein-executed run completes on its own) ·
  invalid_body (400) · payload_too_large (413) · hook_capped (429).
  THE HELPER does all of this in three lines:
      export default g.pipelines.handle(process.env.PIPELINE_SECRET!, async (run, { progress }) => {
        await progress(50, "half way")
        return { text: `made: ${run.params.prompt}` }
      })
  g.pipelines.handle(secret, fn, options?) → (request: Request) =>
  Promise<Response> — a Fetch-API handler (Vercel, Cloudflare Workers,
  Deno, Bun, Node 18+): verifies x-gemmein-signature (401 bad_signature
  before fn ever runs), acks 200 { received: true }, runs fn in the
  background, POSTs its return to /complete or a thrown error's message to
  /fail. If /complete refuses the result itself (400 invalid_body — e.g. an
