  http file URL in the cloud — or 413) the helper ends the run at /fail with
  that refusal ("the pipeline's result was refused (invalid_body): …"), so
  the person's held credits return at once instead of at the deadline; a
  hand-rolled pipeline should do the same. options.waitUntil — the helper cannot detect your host, so pass
  its keep-alive hook or fn's progress is lost silently: Cloudflare
  Workers → ctx.waitUntil; Vercel Node-runtime functions (the default
  for API routes/route handlers) → after() from next/server, or
  waitUntil from @vercel/functions outside Next.js — a Node-runtime
  function freezes after the response same as an edge worker; Vercel
  Edge runtime → its own waitUntil; a long-lived Node/Bun/Deno server →
  nothing. options.toleranceSeconds
  (default 300) widens the signature's clock-drift window. Dedupes
  retried hand-offs on run.id. Standalone export — no app key, no session.
  Locally the same road: the runner posts to your localhost function,
  which calls http://127.0.0.1:<port>/runs/<app>/<env>/<id>/complete.
  CHAINING FROM AN EVENT — a run_started relay ({ "kind": "run_started",
  "tool": "poster" }) fires react-only once ANY tool's run starts, so
  email_person or a start_run action (chaining the next tool for the same
  person) may sit on it; never a hand-off action. This is how an agent runs
  one hop at a time, in a sequence YOUR app composes — Gemmein owns no
  graph of its own and runs none of the agent's code.

  THE STORE ROAD (RevenueCat) — the three templates the Relays room offers,
  and the way an App Store or Play Store purchase reaches Gemmein. It is
  THREE relays, because they take three different actions: a purchase
  fulfils the product, an expiry ends the access, a refund undoes the
  purchase. Each relay has its own URL and its own secret, which goes in
  RevenueCat's Authorization header field (`shared_token` reads the
  `authorization` header). RevenueCat sends that token, not a signature,
  so each relay below carries `"trustUnsignedEvents": true` — ASK THE HUMAN
  before writing it, in plain words (UNSIGNED EVENTS, above).

  Each relay carries its own `when`, so the guard is the RELAY'S OWN, in
  Gemmein, whatever a third party's console is configured to send; an
  event a `when` does not match answers 200 and is not even recorded.
  `when` ANDs its fields, and a field may hold a set with `{ "in": [...] }`.

  - PURCHASE: `{ "event_type": { "in": ["INITIAL_PURCHASE", "RENEWAL",
    "NON_RENEWING_PURCHASE"] } }` → `fulfil_product` with `ref`
    `{{mapped.transaction_id}}`, so a resent event fulfils once. Narrow the
    RevenueCat integration to those three events as well.
  - EXPIRY: `{ "event_type": "EXPIRATION" }` → `revoke_access`. A
    subscription ending is not a refund: the access ends, the credits
    already bought stay.
  - REFUND: `{ "event_type": "CANCELLATION", "cancel_reason":
    "CUSTOMER_SUPPORT" }` (RevenueCat reports a refund as a CANCELLATION
    with that cancel_reason) → `refund_product` with `ref`
    `{{mapped.transaction_id}}`, the reference the purchase relay fulfilled
    it under. It undoes that ONE purchase: the access it granted ends, the
    credits it added come back (never below zero), and its receipt says
    refunded. Access held through any other purchase, such as a
    subscription beside a refunded credit pack, is untouched. A resent
    refund finds the purchase already refunded and moves nothing.

  A cancellation keeps the access until the period ends. RevenueCat sends
  CANCELLATION the moment auto-renew is turned off (cancel_reason
  UNSUBSCRIBE, BILLING_ERROR and the rest) and EXPIRATION when the period
  ends; the plain cancellation matches no revoking relay, answers 200 and
  is not recorded, and the expiry relay takes the access away on
  EXPIRATION.

  The person is named by `person_token`: the app hands RevenueCat the
  person's `storeAccountToken` as the app user id, so neither the gemmein
  person id nor the address enters a third party's ledger. On the Payments
  page, set the product's "How it's sold" to the purchase relay — that is
  what lets it grant a purchase.

      {
        "name": "revenuecat-purchase",
        "trigger": {
          "kind": "receiver",
          "verify": { "scheme": "shared_token", "header": "authorization" },
          "trustUnsignedEvents": true,
          "map": {
            "event_id": "event.id",
            "event_type": "event.type",
            "person_token": "event.app_user_id",
            "product_id": "event.product_id",
            "store": "event.store",
            "transaction_id": "event.transaction_id"
          },
          "when": { "event_type": { "in": ["INITIAL_PURCHASE", "RENEWAL", "NON_RENEWING_PURCHASE"] } }
        },
        "actions": [
          { "type": "fulfil_product", "product": "Pro", "ref": "{{mapped.transaction_id}}" }
        ]
      }

      {
        "name": "revenuecat-expiration",
        "trigger": {
          "kind": "receiver",
          "verify": { "scheme": "shared_token", "header": "authorization" },
          "trustUnsignedEvents": true,
          "map": {
            "event_id": "event.id",
            "event_type": "event.type",
            "person_token": "event.app_user_id",
            "product_id": "event.product_id",
            "store": "event.store"
          },
          "when": { "event_type": "EXPIRATION" }
        },
        "actions": [
          { "type": "revoke_access", "entitlement": "access:pro" }
        ]
      }

      {
        "name": "revenuecat-refund",
        "trigger": {
          "kind": "receiver",
          "verify": { "scheme": "shared_token", "header": "authorization" },
          "trustUnsignedEvents": true,
          "map": {
            "event_id": "event.id",
            "event_type": "event.type",
            "cancel_reason": "event.cancel_reason",
            "person_token": "event.app_user_id",
            "product_id": "event.product_id",
            "store": "event.store",
            "transaction_id": "event.transaction_id"
          },
          "when": { "event_type": "CANCELLATION", "cancel_reason": "CUSTOMER_SUPPORT" }
        },
        "actions": [
          { "type": "refund_product", "product": "Pro", "ref": "{{mapped.transaction_id}}" }
        ]
      }

  A product sold this way names one relay as its road, so a second
  product (a credit pack beside a subscription) gets its own purchase and
  refund relays: the same definitions with the name and "product" changed,
  and the store's product id added to each `when` (`"product_id":
  "<store product id>"`) so each relay acts on its own product's events.

  For another provider's product, the refund relay swaps the trigger's `when` to
  `{ "event_type": "refunded" }` and the action to `refund_product`.
  `g.payments.buy` on a product sold this way answers 409
  `product_not_sellable`, and `g.subscriptions.checkout` on a plan sold
  this way answers 409 `plan_not_sellable`; saving a relay action, a
  product's or a plan's "How it's sold" against a relay name that does not
  exist in this environment answers 400 `relay_missing`. A subscription
  plan sold through such a provider is the same recipe with grant_plan in
  place of fulfil_product and an end-of-access relay running revoke_plan —
  and the Relays room offers that pair as starter text under "A payment
  provider (shared token)": "Payment → grant the plan" (shared_token
  receiver; map event id, email, payment reference; grant_plan with ref =
  that reference) and "Access ended → revoke the plan" (its own webhook
  and secret, a `when` you fill in with the provider's event for the END
  of access — expiry, end of period or a refund, never "will not renew" —
  revoke_plan).
  Change the plan name in the text to the plan's exact name.
  Full depth — every verify scheme, the map and when grammar, the call_url
  contract and signature, every refusal code, the limits and both rails:
  https://docs.gemmein.com/relays (the same chapter is REFERENCE.md
  "## Relays", which the MCP `reference` tool serves).
- Linking records (author on a post, product on an order): store the other
  record's id in a field (`authorProfileId: profile.id`) — in collections
  users write (community, shared, direct) declare it a link field
  (`"authorProfileId": { "type": "link", "link": "profiles" }`); the server
  CHECKS every link points at a real record the writer can read (400
  unknown_record otherwise). Read the linked record back in
  ONE call with expand:
  `list({ expand: ["authorProfileId"] })` → each record gets
  `record.expand.authorProfileId` = the linked record, or null when it was
  deleted or you can't read it — render null as "[deleted]". One level, up
  to 3 fields per call. Never fetch-per-record in a loop — expand does it.
  `where` works on link fields too: one maker's projects =
  `list({ where: { makerProfileId: profile.id } })`. And "the signed-in
  user's own record" in a community collection (their profile) is a keyed
  create: `create(data, { key: "profile:" + user.id })` — one per user by
  construction, and your own retry returns it.
- Images & files: NEVER base64 into record data and NEVER wire up your own
  storage bucket — uploads are built in:
  `const file = await g.collection("posts").upload(blob, { name })`
  → `{ id, ref, contentType, sizeBytes }`. Store `file.ref` (`"file:9f2c…"` — a UUID form)
  in a record field like any text — that's how a record "has" an image or
  a document.
  Store the REFERENCE, never a URL: a reference never expires and grants
  nothing on its own.
  To show or download it: `const { url } = await g.files.link(record.photo)`
  — one call for every file. Pass `{ intent: "download" }` for a download
  rather than a preview. Files in a collection anyone can read get a
  permanent link; every other file gets one that expires within
  minutes, so call `link()` when you render, don't store what it returns.
  Upload permission follows the collection's WRITE rule. This is for
  CUSTOMER uploads through `upload()`, in every collection: images
  (JPEG/PNG/WebP/GIF/HEIC) and documents (PDF/ZIP/EPUB), 25 MB per file;
  audio (mp3, m4a, wav, webm, ogg, flac, aac) up to 100 MB and video (mp4,
  webm, mov) up to 500 MB per file — in Development 25 MB audio and 50 MB
  video. Codec parameters and the usual aliases (`audio/x-m4a`,
  `video/webm;codecs=vp9`) are accepted and stored as the plain type.
  Nothing else here (no SVG, HTML or office files — zip an office file).
  Audio and video are never processed: no transcoding, no thumbnails, the
  bytes you upload are the bytes served. Like every file they are sealed
  (a short-lived signed link) unless the collection is one anyone can
  read, and they PLAY in the page:
  `<video src={(await g.files.link(ref)).url} controls>` (or `<audio>`)
  streams and seeks. Flood limits, per person: 20 audio/video uploads an
  hour; for any file, 5 uploads in progress (started, not confirmed)
  holding at most 1 GB; and a storage share of the larger of 10% of the
  app's storage or 2 GB. An upload in progress holds its declared size
  against that person's share — never the app's storage — until it is
  confirmed or an hour passes, and it can upload at most the size it
  declared. Uploads count toward the app's storage — when you build an
  upload feature, tell your human: "Files your customers upload count toward your app's storage ({ceiling} on your plan); video fills it fastest — you can add 50 GB storage packs under Usage." (see AI
  TOOL MEDIA INPUTS for what {ceiling} is). AI run outputs
  keep their own type — image, audio or video, up to 200 MB each (see
  Runs). A transcribe tool's `file` input takes audio the person uploads
  TO THAT TOOL with `g.ai.upload(tool, file)` (mp3, m4a, wav, webm, ogg,
  flac, codec parameters and the usual aliases accepted, proved by the
  bytes; 25 MB, 14 MB on Google, checked again at run time; sealed to the
  person; refused for any other kind of tool, and 402 when the person
  cannot pay for one run; 60 an hour; an upload no run uses within 24 h
  is deleted), a sealed ref they already own, or an https URL.
  AI TOOL FILE INPUTS (`accepts`). What it is: the kinds of file a person
  may hand an AI tool — image, audio, video, document — each a tick in
  gemmein/ai/tools/<name>.json (`"accepts": ["image", "document"]`) and on
  the dashboard's AI page. What it does: a `type: "file"` input takes the
  ref of a file the person already uploaded (`g.ai.run("describe-photo",
  { photo: upload.ref })`); the server checks kind, model and size before
  anything is spent, then hands the provider a short-lived signed link, the
  bytes inline when small, or (Gemini, over 14 MB) streams it into Gemini's
  Files API — big files are never held in Gemmein's memory. What it does
  NOT do: send a public URL, convert a file, or change the tool's price.
  Needs something else when: the tick must be one the provider + model
  reads — Gemini: image, audio, video, PDF · OpenAI: image (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1,
  gpt-5, o-series), audio (gpt-4o-audio; transcription whisper-1 /
  gpt-4o-transcribe) · Anthropic: image, PDF · AssemblyAI / Deepgram /
  ElevenLabs Scribe: audio, video · Replicate / fal: image, audio, video ·
  Runway: image · your own pipeline: all four; `gemmein dev` and `gemmein
  sync` refuse any other tick and name the models that do. Max per file:
  video 500 MB, audio 100 MB, images and documents 25 MB, or the provider's
  own if lower; `"inputMaxMb": { "video": 200 }` only tightens (config
  only — the dashboard has no size field). Video can cost the founder more
  on their own provider key. A tool that ticks any kind is priced PER RUN —
  a flat credit price per call, the same whatever the file's size; a
  per-token tool with a tick is refused: "A tool that takes files is priced
  per run — set a credit price per call, and lower its file size limit if
  you want to cap your cost." Text-only tools keep per-token. With ticks set, a file input takes only a Gemmein file ref, never a
  raw URL. A tool from before ticks takes exactly what it took. Example: a Gemini chat tool with
  `"accepts": ["video"]` and `inputs: [{ "name": "clip", "type": "file" }]`.
  What happens if… the file's kind isn't ticked → 400 input_not_accepted ·
  the model can't read it → 409 input_not_supported · it's too big → 413
  input_too_large · it's sealed and not this person's → 400 invalid_inputs
  "file not found" · the provider refuses it → 502 input_rejected on a chat
  tool (nothing spent); a run fails with the provider's sentence and
  releases its hold · a second large file while one is still streaming →
  429 input_busy (one per person) · the person can't cover the run's price
  → 402 credits_exhausted before any file is read · a per-token tool ticks a
  kind → refused at `gemmein dev` / `gemmein sync` / the dashboard, priced
  per run instead · the app's storage is full (on Live past its tier's
  grace — the lesser of +10% or 7 days; in Development past twice its
  cap) → uploads are refused with 429 usage_limit_exceeded and a clear message;
  files already stored stay, and runs on them keep working.
  Files a person hands a tool are their uploads, so they count toward the
  app's storage. When you tick a file kind or build an upload feature, tell
  your human: "Files your customers upload count toward your app's storage ({ceiling} on your plan); video fills it fastest — you can add 50 GB storage packs under Usage." {ceiling} is
  the storage ceiling under Usage & billing — on Live the tier's storage
  (5 GB, 50 GB or 150 GB) plus 50 GB for each storage pack; Development is
  capped at 1 GB, whatever the app's Live state.
  Selling an audio file yourself is a product
  delivery file, console-uploaded by the owner (see Products), not a
  customer upload either.
  Images render with `<img>`, audio and video with `<audio>`/`<video>`;
  a document always DOWNLOADS (served as an attachment under the `name`
  you gave upload() — it never opens inside your page), so link documents
  with `{ intent: "download" }`. A Blob you
  built from bytes has no type: pass `{ contentType: "application/pdf" }`
  to upload(), or a 415 says "none declared".
  A file can name ONE other reader:
  `upload(blob, { for: userId })` (addressed/direct collections only) — the
  direct message's attachment; the recipient's `files.link` works, everyone
  else's still refuses. A group chat's attachment names the group: on a
  direct collection `upload(blob, { for: [id, id] })` takes up to 20 people
  (the same list as `create(data, { for: [ids] })`); each one named and the
  uploader can link it and put its ref in a record, everyone else is
  refused. The list is fixed at upload; it counts once, against the
  uploader's share. Without `for`, only the uploader can link it —
  including in a client portal, where the OWNER hands a client a document
  from the dashboard (attach it on the client's record there).
  Files — what happens if…:
  - If a group attachment names more than 20 people → 400
    too_many_recipients; a list on any collection but direct, or an empty
    list → 400 invalid_recipients; someone not in the app → 400
    invalid_audience. Nothing is uploaded.
  - If the direct collection is reply-only → an upload naming anyone who
    has not written to the uploader first is 403 reply_only, exactly as the
    message would be; with messages turned off it is 403 sends_disabled.
  - If one member of the group deletes their account → they leave the
    file's list; the uploader and the others keep it. If the uploader does
    → the file is deleted for everyone.
  - If someone uploads to a collection they can't write to → refused, as
    a record write there would be.
  - If your human makes a collection private or locks it to a plan → its
    files' public links stop opening; link() hands short-lived signed links.
  - If Development rule changes that move files pass 5 a day, or 2 GiB of
    files a day, for one app → a change that makes files public is 429
    development_capped and the rule stays as it was (try again after
    resetAt); making a collection more private is never refused, and Live
    is never refused.
  - If the file is SVG, HTML, an office file or a video/audio format not
    listed (avi, mkv, wma…) → 415 unsupported_file_type; an empty file →
    400 invalid_file.
  - If an image or document is over 25 MB → 413 file_too_large; the
    message states the cap. Audio over 100 MB or video over 500 MB (in
    Development 25 MB and 50 MB) → the same 413, naming the type and the
    environment. A file declared small but uploaded big is caught when it
    is confirmed: refused and discarded.
  - If one person starts more than 20 audio/video uploads in an hour →
    429 media_rate_limited with resetAt; images, documents and other
    people are unaffected.
  - If you have too many uploads in progress — one person with 5 files
    of any type started and not confirmed, or 1 GB of them → the next is
    429 too_many_open_uploads; confirm one, or wait for them to expire an
    hour after they started.
  - If the bytes sent are larger than the size the upload declared →
    the upload itself is refused (the link admits only the declared
    size); confirming it is 400 upload_incomplete.
  - If one person's files would pass their share (the larger of 10% of
    the app's storage or 2 GB, counting uploads in progress) → 429
    person_storage_full; delete some of their files first. Other people
    keep uploading.
  - If Development passes 50 audio/video uploads in 24 hours for one
    app → 429 development_capped with resetAt; Live has no daily count.
  - If an upload is never confirmed → it holds its declared size against
    that person's share for one hour, then lets go; confirming it after that
    is 400 upload_incomplete — upload the file again. The unconfirmed bytes
    are never served and are deleted within a day; the record of the
    upload goes in the nightly cleanup.
  - If the bytes are not the type the file claims (a renamed file — a
    .png called .mp4) → 400 invalid_file_content; the upload is discarded
    and nothing is ever served inline. A retry gets the same answer.
  - If a record field holds a made-up ref or another app's → 400
    unknown_file on create and update.
  - If you link a file in a collection anyone can read → a permanent URL.
    Any other file → a signed link that works for 2 minutes, 5 minutes
    with { intent: "download" }. Call link() when you render.
  - If the person may not see the file → link() is refused: 404 when it
    isn't theirs (as if it did not exist); 403 entitlement_required when
    a plan or product is missing (`err.requires` is the plan's key, the
    one the dashboard shows by name). Show a sign-in or upgrade prompt.
  - If access is revoked after a link was issued → the next link() is
    refused; the issued link works until it expires, and a copy already
    downloaded stays downloaded.
  - If the app's stored files reach 80% and then 100% of its storage →
    your human gets one email at each; on Live, uploads keep working for
    the lesser of +10% or 7 days past it (in Development, up to twice the
    cap), checked with each file's actual size when it is confirmed, then
    429 usage_limit_exceeded.
- Shapes: DECLARING COLLECTIONS — collections your users write (community,
  shared, direct) have a SHAPE — the set of fields allowed — and YOU
  declare it, in the collection's file, before the app writes there.
  Nothing is learned from writes: a test post that happened to be short or
  to carry a poll never becomes a limit. The grammar:
    gemmein/collections/feed.json
    { "rule": "community", "means": "members post updates",
      "fields": {
        "body":   { "type": "text", "maxLength": 2000, "required": true },
        "title":  { "type": "text", "maxLength": 200 },
        "photo":  { "type": "file", "fileClass": "image" },
        "mood":   { "type": "text", "maxLength": 20, "default": "calm" },
        "author": { "type": "link", "link": "profiles" }
      } }
  The file's keys are exactly rule, means, declaredAt, unlockedBy,
  publishing, openFields, directInitiation, fields, rankable — any other is refused
  by name. Each field: `type` ("text", "number", "yesno", "list", "link",
  "json", "file"); `maxLength` (text and list items; leave it out and the
  platform maximum, 32000 characters, applies — choose it from what the
  field is FOR, not from your test data); `required` (default false — a
  create must carry it; updates are patches); `link` (the target
  collection's name, for a link); `fileClass` ("image", "document" or
  "any", for a file); `default` (text, number or yes/no: what records
  without the field show — never with required); `deprecated: true`
  (retired: see below). Up to 30 fields; names are letters, numbers and
  underscores, starting with a letter. `gemmein dev` applies the file at
  once (no restart); `npx gemmein sync` carries it to the cloud app's
  Development (creating the collection, or updating its fields);
  `npx gemmein check` and go-live refuse while any of these collections
  has no fields declared. Private, admin_write, public_read and addressed
  collections take no `fields` (only their writer reads them) — declaring
  some there is refused.
  What Development enforces, exactly as Live does: a write carrying a
  field the file doesn't declare is 400 `undeclared_field` ("feed has no
  field \"x\" — declare it in gemmein/collections/feed.json …" — add it to
  the file, never rename to dodge it); a write to one of these collections
  with no fields declared is 400 `collection_not_declared`; a value of the
  wrong kind, too long, or a required field missing is 400
  `invalid_shape`. Field kinds: text, number, yes/no, list, link (a stored
  record id), json, and FILE — a field that holds an upload()'s ref, of
  the declared class (an image field refuses a ZIP with the teach). The
  file law is UNIVERSAL: on every rule, any top-level field value
  matching the ref grammar must name a real, confirmed file of this app
  that the writer may read — a made-up or foreign ref is refused ("file
  not found", 400 unknown_file). Never invent a ref. (Refs inside list or
  json values aren't judged at write — they still grant nothing at read.)
  If a stored ref's file was later deleted, re-sending it refuses the same
  way: clear the field (null) or upload a fresh file.
  GO-LIVE seals exactly the declared fields into Live — a declared
  collection with no records goes live like any other.
  HOW A LIVE COLLECTION CHANGES: edit the file, sync, and promote (`npx
  gemmein go-live` again, or Promote on the dashboard's Go live page).
  Promote compares the declaration with Live, field by field, and never
  destroys anything:
  - a NEW field is added (one question for your human: what do existing
    records show? — or the declaration's `default` answers it); a field
    declared required joins optional, and the next promote offers the
    tighten below;
  - LOOSER (a bigger maxLength, required → optional, a retired field
    declared again) is applied;
  - TIGHTER (a smaller maxLength, optional → required) first COUNTS the
    live records over the new limit ("12 posts are longer than 500 — the
    longest is 4,000") and applies only with your human's yes — to new
    writes and edits only: existing records are never cut or hidden, and
    an author editing an old long record is told the new limit when the
    edit carries that field. Without the yes, promote refuses
    (`tighten_needs_decision`) and writes nothing;
  - a field marked `"deprecated": true` is RETIRED on Live — never
    deleted: old records keep it and still return
    it; new writes carrying it are refused 400 `field_deprecated`
    ("feed's \"pollOptions\" is retired — new writes can't set it"). The
    same holds in Development the moment the file says so. Retiring is
    EXPLICIT: a Live field simply left out of the file is refused
    (`field_missing_from_declaration`: "feed's \"pollOptions\" is in Live
    but not in gemmein/collections/feed.json — put it back, or mark it
    \"deprecated\": true to retire it") — keep every Live field in the file;
    a promote that names `only` other collections is not stopped by it;
  - a field that CHANGES KIND is refused (`field_type_change`): add a new
    field with the new kind and retire the old one.
  In Live, a 400 invalid_shape names the field that isn't in Live's
  fields or doesn't fit; a new field reaches Live only through a promote
  run, so until then send only the fields Live has. A field promoted with a DEFAULT is served to the
  records that never wrote it: get, list, expand targets and `where`
  filters all see the default (an atomic increment counts from it too),
  and a written value wins; writing `null` clears it back to the default.
  Only text, number and yes/no fields can carry a default; list, link,
  json and file fields join blank. Bound: full-text `search` scans stored
  text only, so a record showing a default is not found by searching for
  it. New collections built in dev reach live through the same PROMOTION,
  with exactly their declared fields; an undeclared one stays in
  Development and the promote list names it.
- Contention (bookings, slugs, stock, shared edits): when two users can race
  for the same thing, a permission model can't save you — preconditions do,
  and they're just arguments on calls you already make. A 409 `conflict` from
  any of them is NOT a failure to retry away: it IS the mechanism working —
  catch it and tell the user the slot/stock/edit was taken.
  - Uniqueness: `create(data, { key: "slot:2026-07-15T15:00" })` — derive the
    key from the thing that must be unique; the second writer gets 409, your
    own retry gets your existing record back (`existing: true`), deleting
    frees the key. That retry IS the lookup — there is no separate
    get-by-key call: to fetch your own record by key later, issue the
    same `create()` with the same key and read `existing: true` off the
    result. It counts as a write (rate and allowance), so use it to
    re-fetch a claim — never on a render path. Keys are unique across
    the WHOLE collection — every writer, every recipient, under every
    safety rule (live records only) — so a claim is race-proof even in
    `direct`/`addressed`. Never
    find-then-create — that races. Keys are 1-120 chars of letters,
    numbers, and `: _ . @ / -` only. A claimed key holds until its record
    is deleted: if a claim must be PAID to stick (book then pay), expiring
    unpaid claims is the owner's job — they delete them from their
    dashboard (a secret key cannot delete records); there is no cron.
  - Limited stock (N units anyone can buy): claim units with keyed creates —
    try `create({...}, { key: "unit:item42:1" })`, on conflict try `:2` … `:N`;
    all taken = sold out. Race-proof under every safety rule.
  - Your own counters: `update(id, { stock: { decrement: 1, floor: 0 } })` —
    the server does the math on current state; breaching the floor/ceiling
    is a 409. (Writes are always owner-scoped: you can't nudge counters on
    OTHER users' records — use the unit-claim pattern above instead.)
  - Shared editing (CMS pages): pass back the version you read —
    `update(id, data, { ifVersion: record.version })`; a stale save gets 409
    instead of silently clobbering someone's edit. Re-read, reapply, retry.
- The owner and the app are separate. Your human's Gemmein account and a
  customer of the app are two different things, even with the same email:
  when your human signs in to their own app, they are an ordinary customer
  — they see only their own records, under every rule, and write only what
  any customer may. There is no "see everyone" option in the app, and no
  `role` to branch on (every session reports `member`). The Gemmein
  dashboard IS the admin dashboard: every customer, every record, every
  message, suspensions, refunds, sends. Build none of that into the app.
- Admin views — only if your human asks for an admin screen INSIDE the app
  (a support desk, a moderation queue), and only this way:
  1. You ask for a server key scoped READ-ONLY to just the collections the
     screen shows (`npx gemmein keys create --access <c>:read,…` — your
     human approves one sentence; or the dashboard's API keys page).
  2. It lives in your server's environment — an API route, a server
     action, a worker — never in the app. `gemmeinServer()` refuses to run
     in a browser or a phone (`secret_key_in_client`), and `npx gemmein
     check` and `go-live` refuse a build that carries a secret key.
  3. Your human sets the admin list: the person ids allowed in, in the
     server's environment (e.g. `ADMIN_PERSON_IDS=usr_…,usr_…`) — ids from
     `verifySession` or the dashboard's Customers page, never emails.
  4. The route verifies the caller, checks the list, then reads with the
     key (the app sends its session token as `Authorization: Bearer` —
     give `gemmein()` a `tokenStore` so your code can read it). An admin
     screen that CHANGES records does it the same way, with a key that
     writes those collections — `g.collection("orders").update(id, {...})`,
     `.create(data, { for: personId })`, `.delete(id)` — on the server:

         // server only
         import { gemmeinServer } from "@gemmein/sdk";
         const g = gemmeinServer(process.env.GEMMEIN_ADMIN_READ_KEY);
         const admins = new Set((process.env.ADMIN_PERSON_IDS ?? "").split(","));
         export async function GET(req) {
           const token = (req.headers.get("authorization") ?? "").replace("Bearer ", "");
           const { person } = await g.verifySession(token);
           if (!admins.has(person.id)) return new Response("not found", { status: 404 });
           const { records } = await g.collection("orders").list({ limit: 50 });
           return Response.json(records);
         }

  Or leave it to the dashboard, which already does all of it — your human
  clicks the record there. Every admin screen your human asks for is a gap
  in the dashboard: tell them to send it with `npx gemmein feedback`.
- Products — a capability card.
  What it is: A named thing you sell once: a download, a licence, a
  credit pack.
  Does: Grants its key and its credits on purchase; writes the buyer's
  receipt; a full refund takes both back. Emails the buyer once per
  payment by default — the purchase email, "Your purchase is ready:
  <product>" ("<n> credits added to your balance" for a credit pack),
  from the domain's account word, linking to the app's Library on its
  verified web domain (the Library path, "/" unless your human sets
  it on the Payments page) and never to the file; it needs a verified
  sending domain and your human can switch it off. Don't build a
  purchase email of your own unless they switch it off. After paying,
  the buyer returns to the app's verified web domain at its return path
  ("/" unless set on the Payments page) with `?paid=<item name>` added
  (the name `buy(name)` / `checkout(name)` took; `gemmein dev`'s simulated
  checkout does the same). THE THANK-YOU MOMENT: when the page loads with
  `paid`, show "Payment received — 100 credits are on their way" (or "Pro
  is on its way"), then re-read `g.credits.balance()` / `g.purchases.mine()`
  / `g.subscriptions.mine()` every 2 seconds for up to 30 seconds until it
  lands, and drop the marker from the URL. The marker is DISPLAY-ONLY:
  anyone can type it — never unlock, grant or count anything on it.
  In the shop, show a product the signed-in buyer already owns (it is in
  `g.purchases.mine()`) as "Owned" with its download, never a second buy
  button.
  Does not: Does not sell subscriptions (those are plans). Sold through
  a relay, it does not set a price — the provider does.
  Needs something else when: You sell through a provider without a
  Payment Link → a relay with fulfil_product; you meter by usage →
  credits spent per AI tool.
  Example: "Starter pack", 100 credits, sold via a GoCardless relay.
  What happens if…
  - If the buyer pays by bank debit → the product is granted only once the payment clears; a failed payment grants nothing. Read `g.purchases.mine()`; never grant on the redirect.
  - If a checkout never clears → it is closed after 30 days; a payment that still arrives is fulfilled.
  - If a purchase is refunded in full → its access and credits are taken back, `g.purchases.mine()` reads `status: "refunded"` with no `delivery`, and `g.files.link` refuses the file from the next call. A copy already downloaded stays with the buyer.
  - If a purchase is refunded in part → access, credits and the file stay; the status reads `part_refunded`.
  - If a buyer who also subscribes is refunded for a product → only what that purchase opened closes. Cancelling a subscription never takes away a product bought outright.
  - If Stripe sends the same payment twice → the product and its credits are granted once.
  - If the product has a `welcomeBonus` → it is added only when this purchase is the buyer's first paid payment in the app ("<product> · welcome bonus"); anyone who paid before (a plan or another product) gets nothing; a purchase that charged nothing (a 100% coupon) adds no bonus; a full refund of the purchase that earned it takes it back.
  - If the page loads with `?paid=` but the purchase is not in `g.purchases.mine()` yet → the webhook has not landed; keep showing "on its way" and re-read. If 30 seconds pass, say "It can take a minute — refresh soon"; never grant on the marker.
  - If the product is sold via a relay or not yet → `g.payments.buy` answers 409 `product_not_sellable`, and `g.payments.products()` does not list it. Show no buy button for it.
  - If a payment lands on a removed product's old Payment Link → nothing is granted, even to a product re-added under that name; the owner's Errors page names it.
  - If a product went on sale before the app's domain was verified → Gemmein points its Payment Link back to that domain the moment it is verified; after paying, the buyer lands on the return path ("/" unless your human sets it on the Payments page; Development and Live each have their own). Nothing to do.
  - If the verified domain is removed → buyers see Stripe's own confirmation page after paying until a domain is verified again. Verify the domain again.
  - If a product is removed → its file stays while any buyer holds it (a purchase not refunded in full — the same rule as the download) and is deleted once nobody does; a file uploaded in the last 24 hours is never touched, and a Live copy replaced at go-live goes the same way. Nothing to do.
- 14-day waiver at checkout — a capability card.
  What it is: One switch per environment, off by default, for one-off
  products: a file, a link, or access alone. Buyers in the UK and EU have
  14 days to cancel an online purchase; for digital content that right
  ends when delivery starts, but only if the buyer agreed to that first.
  Does: With it on, each such product's Stripe checkout shows a box the
  buyer must tick before paying: "I agree to the seller's terms, and I ask
  for this digital content to be delivered straight away. I understand
  that once delivery starts, I lose my right to cancel within 14 days."
  "the seller's terms" links to `termsUrl`, your human's Terms of Service.
  Gemmein makes a new Payment Link for each such product (same price; the
  old link goes off), and every Logs row of the purchase records the
  consent with those words. Turning it off makes links without the box.
  Does not: Does not touch plans or credit packs: they are services used
  over time. The wording is one neutral default and cannot be edited. It
  is not legal advice: your human decides whether it fits their business.
  Needs something else when: Turning it on needs `termsUrl` (https, a
  public domain name — no IP address, localhost or private name — no
  username or password, at most 500 characters); without it the save is
  refused `400 consent_terms_url_required`. Stripe also needs the Terms of
  Service link in the account (Settings → Business → Public details);
  without it turning it on is refused `409 stripe_terms_url_missing`.
  Example: `"consent": { "digitalWaiver": true, "termsUrl":
  "https://example.com/terms" }` in gemmein/payments.json, then
  `npx gemmein sync`.
  Recommend it: when `npx gemmein payments --cloud` says "recommended"
  (the Stripe account is in the UK or EU, or a price is in GBP or EUR),
  tell your human what the buyer will see, and turn it on only when they
  say yes.
  What happens if…
  - If it is turned on → each one-off product (a file, a link, or access alone; not a credit pack) gets a new Payment Link with the box; the old link goes off. `g.payments.buy` hands out the new one at once.
  - If it is turned on without `termsUrl` → refused `400 consent_terms_url_required`, nothing changes. A `termsUrl` that isn't https, carries a username or password, or is over 500 characters is refused `400 invalid_consent`.
  - If `termsUrl` changes while it is on → each such product gets a new Payment Link whose box links the new terms; the old links go off.
  - If a change would make more than 10 new Payment Links in a day in Development (50 in Live) for things already on sale → refused `429 development_capped` (Live: `links_capped`), nothing changes. A new price makes one link; turning this on or off, or a new `termsUrl`, makes one per product it covers; a promote counts the same. A product's first link never counts. Try again the next day (UTC).
  - If your human changed it on the Payments page since your last sync → the next sync shows a conflict and leaves it as they set it, unless they say overwrite (`npx gemmein sync --overwrite`); then change the file to match.
  - If it is on when the app goes live or promotes → the Go live page notes that Live needs a Terms of Service link in the Stripe live account; without one, making Live's links is refused `stripe_terms_url_missing`.
  - If a buyer pays on a link replaced days ago → the payment still resolves to its product.
  - If the app's domain is verified (or its return path changes) while it is on → each link is pointed at the new return in place; the box stays, no link is made again, and nothing counts against the daily cap.
  - If Stripe has no Terms of Service link → turning it on is refused `409 stripe_terms_url_missing` and nothing changes. A product made while it is on is refused the same way.
  - If it is on and a new one-off product is added → its first Payment Link already has the box.
  - If a buyer pays → every Logs row of that purchase carries `consent: { termsOfService: "accepted", text }`, the words they ticked.
  - If a buyer opened checkout on the old link before it was turned on → they can still finish paying, without the box; the purchase is fulfilled, and its Logs rows carry no consent.
  - If it is turned off → the products get new links without the box; purchases already made keep their record.
- Connect Stripe — a capability card. Done in the dashboard, not in code:
  https://docs.gemmein.com/console/payments (the steps are read live at
  https://docs.gemmein.com/llms-dashboard.txt; account safety:
  https://docs.gemmein.com/payments/connect-stripe#protect-your-accounts).
  What it is: A Stripe restricted key, one per environment — `rk_test_…`
  in Development, `rk_live_…` in Live — that your human makes in Stripe
  and pastes in the dashboard. It holds 5 permissions, plus 2 if you sell
  plans (Customer portal and Subscriptions — members manage plans in
  Stripe's portal, and deleting a member ends their subscription); none
  can pay out, refund, or read cards. A product-only app needs the five.
  Adding a first plan later on a five-row key is refused
  (`stripe_key_plan_rows`, naming the two rows) before anything is made;
  `g.subscriptions.manage()` on an app with no plans answers `no_plans`.
  Does: Gives each plan, product and credit pack that has a price a Stripe
  Product, Price and Payment Link, and registers Gemmein's own webhook in
  your human's Stripe, so `g.subscriptions.checkout(plan)` and
  `g.payments.buy(product)` open a Payment Link Gemmein made. A new price
  makes a new Payment Link and turns the old one off. In Live, the
  `rk_live_` key makes Live's own Stripe objects.
  Does not: Pay out, refund, or read cards, customers, charges or
  payments — no permission moves money out of the account. It CAN change
  subscriptions (Subscriptions: Write): Gemmein uses it only to end a
  deleted member's subscription; members switch or cancel their own in
  the portal.
  Take a Stripe secret key (sk_…) or publishable key (pk_…), a Payment
  Link or a signing secret pasted by hand: selling through Stripe needs
  the key, and the door answers `stripe_key_required` ("Connect Stripe on
  the Payments page to sell through Stripe.").
  Needs something else when: You sell through a provider other than
  Stripe → a relay.
  Example: Your human connects a test-mode restricted key on Development's
  Payments page; you declare "pro" at 15 GBP a month in
  gemmein/payments.json and run `npx gemmein sync`;
  `g.subscriptions.checkout("pro")` now opens the Payment Link Gemmein
  made in their Stripe.
- Payments: YOU set how things are sold, in Development, from one file —
  gemmein/payments.json:

      { "plans": [
          { "name": "Free", "default": true,
            "credits": { "perPeriod": 20, "rollover": "none" } },
          { "name": "Pro", "paid": true,
            "price": { "amountMinor": 900, "currency": "gbp", "interval": "month" },
            "credits": { "perPeriod": 500, "rollover": { "carryUpTo": 200 } },
            "welcomeBonus": 50,
            "trial": { "days": 14 },
            "taxCategory": "ai_service" } ],
        "products": [
          { "name": "Field Guide", "price": { "amountMinor": 1500, "currency": "gbp" },
            "deliveryFile": "assets/field-guide.pdf", "taxCategory": "ebook" },
          { "name": "100 credits", "price": { "amountMinor": 500, "currency": "gbp" },
            "grantsCredits": 100 } ] }

  `amountMinor` is in minor units (900 = 9.00); `interval` is day, week,
  month or year (plans only). A product delivers `deliveryFile` (a path
  inside the project: pdf, zip, epub, audio (mp3, wav, m4a, ogg, flac,
  aac) or an image up to 100 MB, or video (mp4, webm, mov) up to 500 MB
  (50 MB in Development) — sync uploads it) or `deliveryUrl` (a link), never both.
  `credits` on a plan is what each paid period grants (`perPeriod`, with
  `rollover` none, carry, or `{ "carryUpTo": n }`; the default plan may
  carry `once`, a welcome allowance); `trial` on a paid plan is a free
  first stretch, once per customer: `days` 1 to 730, `card` "required" (the
  default) or "optional", `credits` the trial grants (absent = the plan's
  `perPeriod` prorated to the trial's days), `onPaymentFailure` "keep" (the
  default: the plan stays while Stripe retries) or "end" (the plan ends at
  once when the first charge fails); `grantsCredits` on a product is what
  each purchase adds. `welcomeBonus` (a plan or a product, 1 to 1,000,000)
  is credits a member gets ONCE, on their first PAID payment — their very
  first paid payment in the app, of whichever plan or product it was,
  that item's bonus; never on a $0 trial start, never again (a renewal, a
  plan switch, a second product, or a bonus turned on after they already
  paid adds nothing). A plan or product granted through a relay
  (grant_plan, fulfil_product) is a payment too: if that came first, it
  was their first payment, and a later Stripe payment brings no bonus.
  The ledger line reads "<name> · welcome
  bonus"; a full refund of that payment takes it back (never below zero),
  a partial one leaves it. Not on the default plan (its welcome is
  `credits.once`). No relay, no server code. `taxCategory` is one of online_service,
  software_subscription, software_subscription_business, ai_service,
  document, ebook, audio, video, artwork, online_course (absent = the
  default for its kind). `sold` is optional: `{ "via": "relay", "relay":
  "<name>" }` or `{ "via": "none" }`; an item with a price is sold through
  Stripe. `npx gemmein dev` sells the file locally (simulated checkout).
  `npx gemmein sync` sets it in the cloud app's DEVELOPMENT and sells it
  straight away: with Stripe connected there, Gemmein makes each priced
  item's test-mode Price and Payment Link; without, each waits "not sold
  yet" and is made the moment your human connects the key. Sync prints its
  plan first (added, changed, removed, conflicts). Sync never touches
  Live — Live gets Development's plans and products at go-live and promote.
  An item missing from the file stays in the cloud; `"remove": true` on
  it takes it down (its Payment Link goes off; a file stays for whoever
  bought it). One sync uploads at most 8 files. Your human may edit any
  plan or product on the Payments page — rows sync set read "set by your
  AI" — and the next sync shows their edit (a rename or "not sold yet"
  included) as a conflict and skips it, unless they say overwrite
  (`npx gemmein sync --overwrite`); when that happens, change the file to
  match their edit: once the file says what the dashboard says (a rename
  included), sync marks it "set by your AI" again, and an old name is free
  for a new item. A plan is checked by the same rules the Payments page
  saves with, so a file the save would refuse (two paid plans, say) is
  refused at the plan, with the reason. `"consent": { "digitalWaiver":
  true, "termsUrl": "https://…" }` at the top of the file turns on the
  14-day waiver at checkout (the "14-day waiver" card below); absent leaves
  it as it is. While Stripe is
  disconnected, an item already made in Stripe is not repriced, renamed
  or removed: the plan says it needs the key. Read back what the cloud has —
  `npx gemmein payments --cloud`: price, how each item is sold, its
  Payment Link, its file (name and size), tax category, and whether Stripe
  is connected and working. What your code sees of it:
  until an environment sells something through Stripe, its checkout answers
  `payments_not_configured` (Live answers it until Stripe is connected in
  Live; going live is still allowed). When the owner turns payments off,
  `g.subscriptions.checkout` and `g.payments.buy` answer 409
  `payments_off` at once: NEW sales stop, and existing customers carry on
  exactly as before — a subscription's renewal keeps its access, and a
  cancellation, a full refund of a purchase, or a renewal Stripe stops
  retrying takes it away. A NEW sale that
  still arrives with nothing to grant is kept whole on the Errors page,
  never dropped and never granted. Only the session's Payment Link names
  what was bought: a payment on a link this environment's key did not make
  is a Problem too, never a grant, whatever its checkout reference says —
  and never a plan by default.
  Going live copies the plans and products into Live (names, prices,
  credit allowances and packs, who they unlock, and each product's file:
  copied into Live's own private product files, so `delivery` in Live
  names Live's copy and a Live buyer's `g.files.link()` mints it; an
  external delivery URL crosses as it is) but never Development's Stripe
  objects, Payment Links or signing secret; Live makes its own once an
  `rk_live_` key is connected there. A product not on sale yet keeps its
  price in Live, changeable before the key is connected. Relays cross
  too, without their secrets: one that needs a secret (a receiver's, or
  the signing secret a `call_url` function checks) arrives paused, with
  the reason — `npx gemmein sync --live` makes Live's own and saves it in
  gemmein/.data/secrets.json ("live"); `email_person` sends from the app's sender domain, which
  Live shares. Once live, `npx gemmein go-live`
  — or Promote on the Go live page; both do the same thing — copies what
  Development has into Live: plans, products and credit packs Live lacks,
  whole (name, price, credits, file), with no Payment Links; plan and
  pack definitions (credits, rollover, welcome allowance, a pack's
  credits) and a product's file brought to Development's (a file already
  copied is not copied again); relays Live lacks; a relay defined
  differently in Live is shown and updated only when your human ticks it
  (`relays: [names]` on the promote); nothing in Live is removed; a
  collection deleted from Live is created again by the next promote, empty,
  with Development's rule; a
  different price is shown, never applied. The CLI sends the payments version it read: if payments changed
  in between, the promote answers 409 and nothing moves — run
  `npx gemmein go-live` again. It also sends the version of Development
  it showed: if Development changed after the review (a sync swapped a
  file, a price, a tool), the promote answers 409 development_changed,
  "Development changed since you reviewed it — review again.", before
  anything is written. A CLI older than this sends no version and is
  answered 428 review_required: "Update the gemmein CLI, then run the
  promote again." An AI tool or collection lock that points
  at a plan Live doesn't have is re-linked by name, and a lock no plan or
  product name can rescue stops the promote before anything moves. AI
  tools Live lacks are copied; one defined differently in Live is shown
  and brought to Development's definition only when your human ticks it
  (`tools: [names]` on the promote, with `toolVersions` — each tool's
  `version` from the dry run; Live keeps its own on/off); a tool
  deleted in Live stays deleted unless ticked back; a tool whose
  provider has no key in Live waits there until it does (`tools: false`
  on the promote leaves tools alone). A provider key is never copied
  unless your human chooses to, in the dashboard or with the CLI's key
  on the promote door (`useSameKey: [provider]`).
  Connecting the key is the one way to sell through Stripe: Gemmein holds
  the signing secret of the endpoint it registered, and hands out only
  the Payment Links it made. A checkout paid by a bank debit opens its
  plan or grants its product only when the payment clears.
  How each paid plan is sold: Stripe (a price, with Stripe connected), a relay (any provider whose webhook
  they map — GoCardless, Lemon Squeezy, Paddle, bank transfer — grants
  it with the `grant_plan` relay action and ends it with `revoke_plan`),
  or not yet. Subscription state is written by Stripe's webhooks OR by
  the relay they configured, never by the app.
  `g.subscriptions.mine()` answers the same
  `{ plan, status }` whichever road wrote it, and `g.subscriptions.checkout`
  on a plan sold via a relay or not yet answers 409 `plan_not_sellable`.
  The app's ONLY checkout job is `await g.subscriptions.checkout("pro")` on the upgrade
  button — Gemmein sends the signed-in user to the right Stripe checkout
  with the buyer and plan wired in. Plans need sign-in (401
  authentication_required signed out); products can be bought signed out. Never build checkout URLs, sessions, or
  Payment-Link redirects yourself (raw emails get silently dropped by
  Stripe's URL rules, and sessions need a secret key that must never ship
  client-side). If g.subscriptions.checkout errors with `plan_has_no_link`,
  give that plan a price in gemmein/payments.json and sync, and ask your
  human to connect Stripe on Development's Payments page. Every checkout and
  buy refusal's message is written for the buyer and safe to show as-is;
  branch on code. In Development the response also carries the owner's fix
  as ownerDetail; Live never does. Plan LIMITS (note
  counts, feature caps) are your app's logic — Gemmein only tells you who is
  on which plan. Gemmein keeps exactly one
  subscription per customer (enforced by the engine, case-insensitive on
  email); cancellations downgrade to the default plan automatically; events
  arriving out of order resolve to the newest. The app reads
  `await g.subscriptions.mine()` → `{ plan, status, trialEndsAt, endsAt }` or
  null (`status` is "trialing", "active" or "cancelled"; `trialEndsAt` while
  a free trial runs, `endsAt` when it is set to cancel), and gates features
  with `sub?.plan === "pro"` — a trialing customer is on the plan.
  CHANGING PLAN: a subscriber never buys a second subscription.
  `g.subscriptions.checkout(plan)` for someone already subscribed answers
  409 `already_subscribed` with `url` (a Stripe customer portal session
  for that member); the app's "Manage plan" button calls
  `await g.subscriptions.manage()`, which navigates there (switch between
  the paid plans — charged or credited at once, a switch during a free
  trial ends the trial — cancel at the end of the period, update the
  card). Gemmein sets the portal up itself from the plans; nothing for
  your human to configure. Never build plan-switch logic in the app;
  Gemmein follows the portal through Stripe's webhook.
  What happens if…
  - If a renewal payment fails → the customer keeps the plan while Stripe retries the card, and `g.subscriptions.mine()` still answers `status: "active"`. Unlock on `plan`; the retry schedule in your human's Stripe is the grace period.
  - If Stripe stops retrying and cancels the subscription or marks it unpaid → the customer moves to the default plan and the plan's access closes. A subscription Stripe leaves past due keeps the plan; your human chooses this in Stripe's subscription settings.
  - If a customer cancels at period end → they keep the plan until the period ends, then move to the default plan.
  - If a subscriber calls `g.subscriptions.checkout` again → no second subscription starts; it answers 409 `already_subscribed` with the customer portal `url` — for every live subscription: active, trialing, past due, unpaid, paused or incomplete. Send them there, or call `g.subscriptions.manage()`.
  - If the same person opens a second checkout for a plan while one is open → 409 `checkout_in_progress` for a few seconds (one open checkout per person per plan); a checkout reference lives 24 hours for anyone else — the person it was made for can still finish paying after that. If two subscriptions still go live, the owner's Problems say "Duplicate subscription — cancel one in Stripe" (Gemmein cannot cancel in Stripe).
  - If `g.subscriptions.manage()` answers 409 `no_subscription` → the signed-in person has never paid for a plan through Stripe; show the plans instead.
  - If `g.subscriptions.manage()` answers 409 `no_plans` → the app sells no plans (none listed, and no subscription still charging); a plan removed while members still pay keeps their portal open.
  - If `g.subscriptions.manage()` answers 503 `portal_unavailable` → Gemmein couldn't read the app's payments for a moment; nothing changed — let them try again.
  - If `g.subscriptions.manage()` answers 409 `portal_unavailable` → the portal can't open right now (Stripe not connected here, or the key lacks Customer portal: Write); the message is safe to show, and in Development `ownerDetail` says what your human fixes on Payments.
  - If a member deletes their account → every Stripe subscription they bought (whichever Stripe customer it is on — a Payment Link makes one per checkout) is set to cancel at the end of the period (they are never charged again; nothing is refunded) and Logs says so; one still owing or never paid (past due, unpaid, incomplete) is cancelled at once, no refund — Stripe then stops collecting its open invoices; if Stripe refuses, your human gets an alert to cancel it in Stripe.
  - If deleting an account answers 503 `erase_unavailable` → Gemmein couldn't read the app's payments for a moment, so nothing was deleted and nothing changed in Stripe; show the message and let them try again.
  - If `g.subscriptions.manage()` answers 429 `portal_rate_limited` → the member opened it more than 10 times in 10 minutes (Development also caps an app at 100 an hour); show the message and let them try again later.
  - In `npx gemmein dev` → `manage()` opens a local page saying what Stripe's portal would offer; nothing changes.
  - If a subscriber changes plan in the customer portal (or the price is changed in Stripe to another plan's price) → the plan moves and access follows. Credits mirror net money, both ways: moving up grants credits when the upgrade is PAID — each prorated line on the invoice is priced on its own: a line for the new plan grants that plan's per-period credits × the share of the period it covers, a line for the old plan takes its credits back the same way, each line by its own discounts (tax excluded; money from the customer's Stripe balance counts; a line in another currency than its plan grants nothing), so a 99% coupon gives 1% and several changes on one invoice each count once — and if the owner's portal bills prorations later, they come with that invoice; a trialing switch pays nothing and grants nothing extra. Moving down (or a refund of the upgrade, in proportion) takes back credits at the same rate for the money returned: first from what that upgrade granted, never from a credit pack's own line; the ledger records it as a plan change, not a refund.
  - If a downgrade returns money for credits you already used → your balance goes below zero until your next renewal or purchase. A balance below zero can't be spent (spends, AI calls and runs answer `credits_exhausted`); the next renewal or pack pays it down first, and credits you still hold count against it. A price Gemmein did not make leaves the plan as it is.
  - If a renewal and a plan change arrive out of order → the renewal grants the credits of the plan on its own invoice.
  - If a subscription is paused in Stripe → the customer is on the default plan while paused; when it resumes, the plan comes back.
  - If a customer starts a free trial → the plan opens at once with its trial credits; `mine()` answers `status: "trialing"` and `trialEndsAt`. One trial per customer per app (a +tag or Gmail dot is the same customer; a catch-all domain's many addresses are many customers — use card-required, the default, to guard against that), none for anyone who has paid for a plan, and deleting the account does not give a second one; checkout sends them to the paid link instead.
  - If a trial ends because the customer switched plan → the new plan's first period's credits are granted when that switch is paid.
  - If the trial ends and the card pays → `status` becomes "active" and the first paid period's credits are granted.
  - If the trial ends and the card is declined → with `onPaymentFailure` "keep" the plan stays while Stripe retries; with "end" the customer moves to the default plan at once, and the plan opens again if a retry succeeds.
  - If a card-optional trial ends with no card → Stripe cancels it and the customer moves to the default plan. Send trialling customers to `g.subscriptions.manage()` to add a card.
  - If a customer cancels during the trial → they keep the plan until the trial ends and are never charged; `mine().endsAt` says when.
  - If Development has given 25 free trials today → checkout hands out the paid link until the day rolls on; Live has no cap.
  - If a subscription payment is refunded in full → that period's credits are taken back (and the welcome bonus, if that payment granted it) and the payment and its receipt read `refunded`; the plan and its access stay.
  - If the plan has a `welcomeBonus` → it lands once, with the member's first PAID payment in the app (the first invoice that charged anything — a first charge after a free trial, or an upgrade's proration — a $0 trial start grants none) — and only if they never paid before (a bonus turned on later never pays existing payers); renewals and plan switches add nothing.
  - If a subscription invoice is paid → a receipt is written for it in the receipts collection (when the app keeps one): { kind: "subscription", plan, status, amountTotal, currency, paidAt, paymentRef } — one per invoice that charged something (first payment, each renewal, a paid upgrade); a $0 invoice or a downgrade's credit invoice writes none. A purchase's receipt carries kind "purchase". A relay or an app watching receipts for purchases filters with `where: { kind: "purchase" }` (subscriptions: "subscription").
  - If a bank-debit checkout never clears → it is closed after 30 days; a payment that still arrives opens the plan.
- Paid ACCESS (entitlements): a collection can be locked to a plan or
  product — your human picks it BY NAME in the "Unlocked by" row on the
  Data page (several allowed; any one of them opens it), or, in
  local dev, you write the same thing as `"unlockedBy": ["pro"]` in
  gemmein/collections/<name>.json (names, never keys; `npx gemmein check`
  checks that the lock holds and names collections left open while the app
  sells something — unless what it sells is an AI tool gated by a plan or
  product, or priced in credits the app sells: the free-core, paid-AI
  shape, which it reports as a note, not a warning) — and the
  engine refuses customers without it, under every rule (app_only refuses
  every app session regardless — "unlockedBy" is refused there). (Server
  secret keys and the owner's dashboard are exempt by design; link/expand
  silently hide gated records rather than naming them.) Every plan and
  product carries its own key, DERIVED from its name the first time it is
  saved: `access:` + the name lowercased, with every run of anything that
  is not a letter or a digit turned into ONE dash, trimmed at both ends
  (plan "pro" → `access:pro`; product "Pro Max" → `access:pro-max`; "Deep
  Research!" → `access:deep-research`). It is minted ONCE and stored, so a
  later rename keeps the key and nothing a customer holds moves. Never
  build the key yourself from a name you have in hand — pass the NAME and
  let the server resolve it. The paid webhook grants that key, and a FULL refund or a
  cancellation revokes exactly what it granted — nothing else. A partial
  refund leaves access in place.
  Owners also grant and revoke by hand (trials, comps, support). Effective
  access is the UNION of a customer's live grants. A signed-in customer
  without access gets `403 entitlement_required`: `err.requires` is the
  plan's key (the dashboard shows the plan by name; the key is
  `access:<slug>`).
  A collection unlocked by several plans (OR) still names ONE key — offer
  your plans by name through checkout, never a key list. Show your upgrade
  screen and send them to checkout; retry only after they hold one. Proof surfaces: `await g.purchases.mine()`
  (everything they paid for, refunds applied, with the `grants` each purchase
  carries) and `await g.subscriptions.mine()`.
  Access is yes-or-no. A QUANTITY beside it is credits — buy a pack, spend
  atomically, a zero floor (see Credits): a "100 credit pack" is a product
  with Grants credits = 100, and the ledger ADDS at every purchase, so a
  second pack makes 200. NO seats, by design — not coming.
- Three FAMILIES of grant (seven sources), and the lines between them are
  law. Every grant is one key + one reason + a start + maybe an end, never
  edited (an extension is a NEW grant). PURCHASE-TIED (`subscription`,
  `purchase`): written only when money arrives — by Stripe's signed
  webhook, or by the relay action (`fulfil_product`, `grant_plan`) the
  owner set as how that product or plan is sold — never by the owner's
  hand, never by your app; a subscription grant ends on cancellation,
  lapse or its relay's `revoke_plan`, a purchase grant on a FULL refund
  (partial leaves it); the only grants that count as revenue. Revoking one
  by hand stops the access and refunds nothing. BY-HAND (`manual`,
  `trial`, `promotion`, plus `migration` for customers imported from
  elsewhere): the owner writes them from a customer's page, or your server
  with a secret key (`grantAccess`) — plan or product BY NAME, optional end
  date, a reason — and they end on that date or when revoked; never
  revenue; a refund never touches them. BY RELAY (`relay`): a relay's
  `grant_access` action writes it when its trigger fires (a provider's
  signed webhook, a schedule, a record change) — no secret key can create
  one; it ends on the date the action named or when revoked; never
  revenue; a refund never touches it. Effective access is the union of all
  three families. WHEN A REFUND MEETS ACCESS, THE OWNER DECIDES: the platform
  revokes only on events that plainly mean it (subscription cancelled or
  lapsed; one-off purchase refunded IN FULL). A partial refund leaves
  access; a refund on a subscription invoice touches no access at all
  (grants are revoked by purchase reference, subscriptions by customer).
  A cancel-at-period-end keeps access until the period ends. If the owner
  wants access gone NOW, they cancel the subscription immediately in
  Stripe or revoke by hand on the customer's page — both audited; every
  refund the webhook chose not to act on is written to the activity view.
  Tell your human this when they ask "I refunded them, why can they still
  get in" — never write refund logic in the app. Your app sees purchases (`g.purchases.mine()`, each with its
  `grants`) and the subscription (`g.subscriptions.mine()`) — by-hand
  grants are NOT listed to the app; a gated read still succeeds. So never
  rebuild the paywall client-side from what you can list: let the server
  refuse and show the upgrade prompt on `entitlement_required`. "Give X a
  free month" is a trial grant on their customer page, never code — ask
  your human.
- Selling THINGS (one-off purchases — a beat, an ebook, a course; DIGITAL
  access only — physical goods, shipping, inventory and carts are out of
  scope, said out loud): plans are for subscriptions; products are for
  things. Selling a SERVICE session this way (tutoring, coaching, a
  consultation) is fine — nothing ships; the recorded purchase is the
  proof the session was paid for. You declare products in the same
  gemmein/payments.json and set how each is sold: Stripe (a price, with Stripe
  connected), a relay
  (any provider whose webhook the founder maps — GoCardless, Lemon
  Squeezy, Paddle, bank transfer — fulfils it with `fulfil_product`), or
  not yet (the product is defined, its grants and credits are known, no
  road wired). The app calls
  `await g.payments.buy("beat")` — or, when one product covers many items (license
  tiers over a catalog), names the item:
  `await g.payments.buy("premium license", { item: "beat_37" })` (display text
  only; the PRICE is always the Payment Link's or the relay's, so the
  item note can never change what's paid). A product
  sold via a relay or not yet has no Payment Link to open:
  `g.payments.buy` answers 409 `product_not_sellable`.
  GUESTS CAN BUY PRODUCTS. `g.payments.buy` works signed in or signed
  out — never put a sign-in wall in front of a product's buy button.
  Signed out, Stripe Checkout asks for the buyer's email, and the purchase
  is theirs the first time they sign in with that same email
  (`g.purchases.mine()`, the Library). Only an `item` note needs a
  signed-in buyer (401 `authentication_required` otherwise). PLANS NEED
  SIGN-IN: `g.subscriptions.checkout` signed out answers 401
  `authentication_required` — a plan is tied to an account, so send the
  person to sign in first. THE PURCHASE EMAIL is ON by default: after a paid product
  purchase (a Payment Link or a relay's fulfil_product) Gemmein emails the buyer, once per payment, "Your purchase is ready: <product>" (a credit pack: "<n> credits added to your balance", about the balance) — and when a
  plan or its free trial starts from a checkout, once per subscription, "Your <plan> trial has started" (when it ends, the price after it,
  "cancel any time before <date> and you won't be charged") or "You're on <plan>" (the price, renewing automatically) — the trial's end is
  Stripe's own; the price is always the plan's REGULAR price, never a discounted one; a discount on the subscription adds one line from
  Stripe ("Your discount applies until <date>", "… applies to one payment", "… has no end date"), or none when Stripe can't be asked — both pointing to
  the member's account page in your app, where `g.subscriptions.manage()` opens the portal — from your
  verified domain's account address, linking to your Library (your app's
  verified web domain + a path, "/" unless the founder sets one on
  Payments → Products) — never to the file. With no verified sending
  domain or web domain it is not sent (never from a Gemmein address
  instead), and Logs says so once a day ("needs a verified domain") — a
  test member in Development still gets it, in the test mailbox, without
  the link until the web domain is verified. An
  erased buyer who buys again is a new customer; a payment begun before
  the erasure grants nothing. Keys starting "gemmein:" are reserved
  (notify answers 400 reserved_key). Don't build a purchase-email relay or
  send one from your code; the founder turns Gemmein's off on Payments →
  Products if they want their own. Gemmein records every completed
  payment itself — `await g.purchases.mine()` is the buyer's proof:
  { item, kind, status: "paid"|"part_refunded"|"refunded", amountMinor,
  currency, refundedMinor, grants, paidAt, delivery? }. Selling a FILE (a
  beat, an ebook, a sample pack, a course video — pdf, zip, epub, audio or
  an image up to 100MB, video (mp4, webm, mov) up to 500MB, 50MB in
  Development): the founder attaches it directly on the product
  card — upload, right there, no receipts collection required. The buyer's
  purchase carries `delivery: { type: "gemmein_file", file }`; resolve the
  ref with `g.files.link(file, { intent: "download" })` — or, for an
  audio or video product, `g.files.link(file)` into `<video>`/`<audio>`:
  it plays in the page. The purchase IS
  the authorization, re-checked on every mint: a refund cuts the file off
  the moment it lands, a partial refund does not, and a saved ref or an
  expired URL grants nothing on its own. A receipts collection (rule
  `addressed`) remains OPTIONAL, for proof records only. External
  `delivery: { type: "external_url" }` is a plain handover: Gemmein
  controls who is TOLD, not who can use it. Gate fulfilment on the
  purchase or the entitlement it granted, never on the redirect coming
  back — redirects can be faked; the record comes from Stripe's signed
  webhook. NO carts, NO quantities — one product per checkout by design; a
  cart is N checkouts or one bundled product. 404 unknown_product means
  the name your app sent isn't a product in this environment — check the
  name; the buyer sees "That item isn't available.", and the owner's Logs
  list what this environment sells (in Development the response also
  carries it as ownerDetail).
- The catalog — what the app sells. See https://docs.gemmein.com/payments
  What it is: Payments → Products and Plans in the dashboard, read by the
  app. `await g.payments.products()` for a storefront and
  `await g.subscriptions.plans()` for a pricing page — one public read
  (GET /catalog) with the publishable key, no sign-in needed, each in the
  dashboard's order.
  Does: lists exactly what `g.payments.buy(name)` and
  `g.subscriptions.checkout(name)` would sell right now, plus the free
  plan. A product is { name, price: { amountMinor, currency }, delivers:
  "file" | "link" | "none", credits: number | null, unlocks: string[] }; a
  plan is { name, free, price: { amountMinor, currency, period }, credits:
  { perPeriod, once } | null, unlocks: string[] } — the free plan is
  `free: true`, price 0, period null. Prices are minor units (1500 =
  15.00). Development and Live each answer their own.
  Does not: list an item that is not sold yet, sold through a relay, or
  waiting for Stripe to be connected; carry a Payment Link, a Stripe id, a
  file, a delivery link or anything of another environment; carry
  descriptions or pictures — those are your app's design.
  Needs something else when: the storefront wants words and images per
  item (keep them in your code, keyed by `name`, e.g. a `copy` object;
  a name the catalog does not list is simply not shown); someone buys
  (`buy` / `checkout`); you need what a person OWNS (`g.purchases.mine()`,
  `g.subscriptions.mine()`).
  Example: `const products = await g.payments.products();` then render
  each with `COPY[p.name]` for its words and image and a Buy button that
  calls `g.payments.buy(p.name)`. NEVER create a `products` (or `plans`)
  collection to list what you sell: the founder would have to fill both
  and keep names and prices in sync by hand.
- Credits — a quantity beside access. See https://docs.gemmein.com/credits
  What it is: a balance your customers hold and your product spends — a
  pack they buy, a plan's allowance each paid period, the free plan's
  allowance each month (or once, as a welcome), a comp you give, an
  AI tool call priced in credits. Every credit sits on a GRANT (pack ·
  plan-period · comp · promo · refund); the balance is what is left on the
  live ones; spends burn comps and promos first, then allowances, then
  packs, so bought credits go last.
  Does: a product grants credits at purchase (its Grants credits field); a
  plan grants them each paid period with the owner's rollover rule (carry
  · none · carry up to n); the free (default) plan grants its allowance
  once per person per calendar month (UTC), at their first spend that
  month — never by a job over everyone; every balance read shows it as
  spendable before it lands — and its `once` welcome allowance to a
  person who never held a paid plan; your server spends them with a reason; the AI
  route spends the credits the owner set for the named tool, one by
  default; a relay grants them (optionally for a number of days) and can
  fire when someone runs low (trigger credits_low: a spend, a clawback,
  an expiry — never a rise); the owner's dashboard
  shows the meter, the grants, the ledger and comps by hand with an
  optional expiry. Every movement is one ledger line.
  Does not: expire packs (an allowance with no rollover ends with its
  period — at the period end a Stripe invoice names, else when the next
  period lands; a promo with days and a comp with a date end on time —
  one `expire` line per grant); go negative
  (floor 0 — a spend past the balance is refused whole, never partly);
  open access (that is an entitlement — a person with 500
  credits and no plan is still refused by a locked collection); count
  seats or quotas; spend from the browser.
  Needs something else when: access should switch on with a plan (an
  entitlement — see Paid ACCESS); you bill by usage after the fact (not
  shipped — sell packs up front); the spend must happen in the browser
  (it never does: your server, a relay or the AI route moves credits).
  The case: "sell a 100-credit pack and let each chat cost one". The pack
  is a product in gemmein/payments.json with `"grantsCredits": 100`; each purchase ADDS 100 to the buyer's
  balance (two packs make 200), and a FULL refund claws back what is still
  unspent, floor 0. The app reads the balance to show it:

      const { balance, reserved, expiring } = await g.credits.balance()   // browser, signed in
      // balance = spendable now · reserved = held by runs and per-token AI calls in flight ·
      // expiring = { credits, at } for the soonest credits that will die, or null

  Your server spends by person id, with a reason and a key, so a retry
  never spends twice (the key needs "Spend a person's credits" ticked):

      const server = gemmeinServer(process.env.GEMMEIN_SECRET_KEY!)   // once, at module scope
      const r = await server.spendCredits(person.id, {
        amount: 1, reason: "export", key: `export:${jobId}`
      })
      // { ok: true, spent: 1, deduped: false, balance: { before: 12, after: 11 },
      //   event: { id: "cev_…", reason: "export", actor: "<the key's name>" } }
      // the same key again: spent: 0, deduped: true, the same event, nothing moved
      // 402 credits_exhausted — "this person has 0 credits — the spend needs 1"

  `holdings.credits` is the same meter on verifySession and holdings, so one
  verify answers who, what they hold AND how many. Numbers: packs never
  expire · floor 0 · a person holds at most 1,000,000,000 (spendable and
  reserved together) · a pack 1..1,000,000 · a server spend 1..10,000 per
  call · a comp ≤100,000 · a relay grant 1..10,000 · spend lines kept 90
  days on the cloud rail (purchases, grants, expiries and clawbacks are
  kept). Facts: a purchase by an email that has never
  signed in creates the person and credits them; your `key` is scoped to
  the person and namespaced (`srv:`), so one order id reused for two people
  charges both and rotating the secret key never re-charges; a full refund
  claws back what THAT purchase's ledger row granted, whatever the product
  says today; the owner's page lists the newest 50 non-spend lines and the
  credits the person spent in the last 30 days. Codes: `credits_exhausted`
  (402 — carries the balance; show the pack, never retry the spend) ·
  `capability_required` (403) · `person_not_found` (404) · `invalid_amount`
  / `invalid_reason` / `invalid_key` (400) · `dedupe_conflict` (409 — the
  key already names a different movement) · `credits_ceiling` (409 — the
  balance would pass 1,000,000,000; nothing added).
  What happens if…
  - If a spend is more than the balance → 402 `credits_exhausted`, refused whole; nothing moves. Show the pack; never retry the same spend.
  - If the same spend is sent twice with the same key → it is spent once; the repeat answers `deduped: true`.
